chapters.title: And These Are the Names
chapters.html:
Exodus 1

1And these are the names of the sons of Israel coming to Egypt with Jacob, each man and his household they came:

2Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah;

3Issachar, Zebulun, and Benjamin;

4Dan and Naphtali, Gad and Asher.

5And all the souls who came out of Jacob's loins were seventy souls. And Joseph was in Egypt.

6And Joseph died, and all his brothers, and all that generation.

7And the sons of Israel were fruitful and swarmed and multiplied and grew numerous beyond measure, and the land was filled with them.

A New King

8And a new king rose over Egypt, who did not know Joseph.

9And he said to his people, "Look — the people of the sons of Israel are more numerous and stronger than we are.

10Come, let us deal shrewdly with them — otherwise they will multiply, and it will happen that if war breaks out they will be added to those who hate us, and fight against us, and go up out of the land."

11And they set over them chiefs of forced labor, to afflict them with their burdens. And they built store cities for Pharaoh: Pithom and Rameses.

12But the more they afflicted them, the more they multiplied and the more they broke out. And they dreaded the sons of Israel.

13And Egypt made the sons of Israel serve with crushing labor.

14And they made their lives bitter with hard service — in mortar and in bricks, and in every service in the field — all their service in which they made them serve, with crushing labor.

Shiphrah and Puah

15And the king of Egypt said to the Hebrew midwives, of whom the name of one was Shiphrah and the name of the second was Puah,

16and he said, "When you deliver the Hebrew women, look at the two stones: if it is a son, put him to death, and if it is a daughter, she may live."

17And the midwives feared God, and they did not do as the king of Egypt spoke to them, and they let the boys live.

18And the king of Egypt called for the midwives and said to them, "Why have you done this thing, and let the boys live?"

19And the midwives said to Pharaoh, "Because the Hebrew women are not like the Egyptian women — they are vigorous. Before the midwife comes to them, they have given birth."

20And God did well by the midwives, and the people multiplied and grew very numerous.

21And it came to pass, because the midwives feared God, that He made them households.

22And Pharaoh commanded all his people, saying, "Every son that is born, throw him into the Nile, and every daughter you may let live."

Notes

  • v1 "And these are the names" — ve-elleh shemot, and the book starts with and. It does not begin; it continues, picking up Genesis 46:8, which opened its own list with almost the same words. The Hebrew name of this book is Shemot, Names, taken from this first line — so the book English calls Exodus is called Names by the people whose book it is.

  • v1 "each man and his household" — ish u-veito, the distributive ish again: each one with his own. The same construction that made Genesis 7:2 look, in English, as though the animals were married.

  • v5 "seventy souls" — the figure from Genesis 46:27, and yots'ei yerekh Ya'aqov, those who came out of Jacob's loins, is that chapter's phrase too (46:26). The last verse of Genesis put Joseph in a coffin in Egypt; the fifth verse of Exodus says and Joseph was in Egypt, and then kills him in the next line. The seam is deliberate and it is only two verses wide.

  • v7 five verbs, and all of them are creation's — paru va-yishretsu va-yirbu va-ya'atsmu bi-me'od me'od. Fruitful and multiply are the blessing of Genesis 1:28. Swarmed, sharats, is the word for what the waters do on the fifth day, 1:20–21 — used here of people. And va-timmale ha-arets otam, the land was filled with them, is 1:28's fill the earth, arriving at last.

    It is also the promise to Abraham coming true. Va-ya'atsmu is atsum, the word of Genesis 18:18 — a great and numerous nation. The blessing reaches its fulfilment in the first paragraph of the book about slavery, and that fulfilment is precisely what the next verse treats as a problem.

  • v8 "who did not know Joseph" — asher lo yada et Yosef, and yada, to know, is the verb Genesis ran on: Adam knew Eve, Joseph made himself known to his brothers. A whole book of knowing ends, and the new reign begins with a man who does not.

  • v9 "more numerous and stronger than we are" — rav ve-atsum mimmennu, and atsum is the same word as v7 and as the promise in Genesis 18:18. Pharaoh is quoting God's blessing back as a threat, without knowing it. He is the first person in the Bible to be frightened by a promise.

  • v10 "let us deal shrewdly" — nitchakkemah, from chakham, to be wise. Egypt's answer to a divine promise is a policy meeting. And the plan's stated fear is not that they will rise up but that they will leave: ve-alah min ha-arets, and go up out of the land — alah, the verb God used to Jacob in Genesis 46:4, I will surely bring you up. Pharaoh's nightmare and God's promise are the same sentence.

  • v11 "Pithom and Rameses" — Genesis 47:11 settled Jacob's family in the best of the land, in the land of Rameses, as a gift. Four hundred years later the same name is a store city they are whipped into building. Genesis never points this out. Exodus does not either. The word simply comes back.

  • v12 "the more they afflicted them, the more they multiplied and the more they broke out" — yifrots, from parats, to burst through a wall — the verb of Jacob's wealth in Genesis 30:43 and of the baby who shoved past his brother to be born in 38:29. Oppression is applied and the response is the creation blessing again, harder. Then va-yaqutsu, they dreaded them, a verb that carries loathing and sickness at once.

  • vv13, 14 "crushing labor" — be-farekh, twice, framing the sentence. Perekh is rare and its force is harshness or breaking; the word itself is hard to say. And va-yemareru et chayyeihem, they made their lives bitter — marar. Eleven chapters later, at the first Passover, Israel is told to eat the lamb with bitter herbs, merorim, from this root. The meal remembers the word.

  • v15 the midwives are named, and the king is not — Shiphrah and Puah. The most powerful man on earth is the king of Egypt and then Pharaoh, a title, never a name. Two midwives who disobey him are named twice each. The text records who it thinks is worth remembering.

  • v16 "the two stones" — ha-ovnayim, the same word Jeremiah 18:3 uses for a potter's wheel: a physical object, likely a birth-stool. The phrase just marks the point in delivery when the child's sex became visible.

  • v17 "and the midwives feared God" — the first recorded disobedience of a king in the Bible, and the reason given is fear of God rather than courage or pity. They are not Israelites by anything the text says; they are called the Hebrew midwives, which can mean midwives who are Hebrew or midwives to the Hebrews, and the Hebrew will not decide.

  • v19 "they are vigorous" — ki chayot hennah. Chayah is the ordinary word for a living creature, and in Genesis it is the word for beasts as opposed to livestock. So the sentence they feed Pharaoh is either they are full of life or, said to a man who already despises them, they are like animals. He accepts it. The midwives may be lying, flattering his contempt, or both, and the text does not say.

  • v21 "He made them households" — va-ya'as lahem battim. God gives the two women who preserved other people's children families of their own. Bayit, house, is also a dynasty in Hebrew — what David is promised in 2 Samuel 7.

  • v22 "throw him into the Nile" — ha-ye'orah, the Egyptian loanword for the Nile that Genesis 41 used for Pharaoh's dream. The river that made Egypt rich in Joseph's story is turned into a method of disposal. And the command is given to all his people, not to officials — every Egyptian is now deputized.

chapters.title: Because I Drew Him Out of the Water
chapters.html:
Exodus 2

1And a man from the house of Levi went and took a daughter of Levi.

2And the woman conceived and bore a son. And she saw him, that he was good, and she hid him three months.

3And she could hide him no longer, and she took for him a basket of papyrus and daubed it with tar and with resin, and put the child in it, and set it in the reeds on the bank of the Nile.

4And his sister stationed herself at a distance, to know what would be done to him.

5And Pharaoh's daughter came down to bathe at the Nile, and her young women were walking beside the Nile. And she saw the basket among the reeds, and she sent her maid and took it.

6And she opened it and saw him — the child — and here, a boy crying. And she had compassion on him, and said, "This is one of the Hebrews' children."

7And his sister said to Pharaoh's daughter, "Shall I go and call you a nursing woman from the Hebrews, and she will nurse the child for you?"

8And Pharaoh's daughter said to her, "Go." And the girl went and called the child's mother.

9And Pharaoh's daughter said to her, "Take this child away and nurse him for me, and I myself will give your wages." And the woman took the child and nursed him.

10And the child grew, and she brought him to Pharaoh's daughter, and he became a son to her. And she called his name Moses, and said, "Because I drew him out of the water."

He Turned This Way and That

11And it came to pass in those days that Moses grew up, and he went out to his brothers and saw their burdens. And he saw an Egyptian man striking a Hebrew man, one of his brothers.

12And he turned this way and that, and saw that there was no one around, and he struck down the Egyptian and hid him in the sand.

13And he went out on the second day, and here — two Hebrew men fighting. And he said to the one in the wrong, "Why do you strike your neighbor?"

14And he said, "Who made you a chief and a judge over us? Are you saying you will kill me as you killed the Egyptian?" And Moses was afraid and said, "Surely the thing is known."

15And Pharaoh heard this thing and sought to kill Moses. And Moses fled from before Pharaoh and settled in the land of Midian. And he sat down by a well.

The Well in Midian

16And the priest of Midian had seven daughters. And they came and drew water and filled the troughs to water their father's flock.

17And the shepherds came and drove them off, and Moses rose and saved them, and watered their flock.

18And they came to Reuel their father, and he said, "Why have you come so quickly today?"

19And they said, "An Egyptian man delivered us from the hand of the shepherds, and he even drew, drew water for us, and watered the flock."

20And he said to his daughters, "And where is he? Why did you leave the man? Call him, and let him eat bread."

21And Moses decided to stay with the man, and he gave Zipporah his daughter to Moses.

22And she bore a son, and he called his name Gershom, for he said, "I have been a foreigner in a foreign land."

23And it came to pass in those many days that the king of Egypt died. And the sons of Israel groaned from the labor and cried out, and their cry for help went up to God from the labor.

24And God heard their groaning, and God remembered His covenant with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob.

25And God saw the sons of Israel. And God knew.

Notes

  • v2 "she saw him, that he was good" — va-tere oto ki tov hu, and that is the sentence of the first day of creation: and God saw the light, that it was good (Genesis 1:4). A mother looking at a baby she is about to hide gets the words God used looking at the light.

  • v3 "a basket of papyrus" — the Hebrew is tevat gome, and tevah is the word for Noah's ark. It occurs in the Bible for those two objects and nothing else. Both are containers, not boats; both are sealed against water — Noah's covered with covering, this one daubed with tar and resin; both carry a survivor through a flood sent to kill. The second one is three feet long.

  • v3 "in the reeds" — ba-suf. The sea Israel walks through in 13:18 is Yam Suf, the Sea of Reeds. The child is hidden among the suf and will bring a nation out through the suf, and Hebrew says it with the same word both times.

  • v5 "Pharaoh's daughter came down to bathe at the Nile" — her father has just made the Nile an instrument for drowning boys (1:22). She goes down to it, finds one of them, and takes him home. The text lets the two sentences sit four verses apart without comment.

  • v6 "This is one of the Hebrews' children" — she knows exactly what she is doing, says so out loud, and does it anyway. She is the daughter of the man whose policy it is.

  • v9 "I myself will give your wages" — the baby's own mother is hired, and paid by the palace, to nurse her own son; v8 names her outright, em ha-yeled, the child's mother — information given to the reader, not a claim about what Pharaoh's daughter knows or works out. She was given plain interior thoughts one verse earlier, she had compassion... this is one of the Hebrews' children (v6), and is given none here, at the exact point where it would matter. The sister arranged the whole thing in a single sentence (v7), and nobody in the scene is named except the child, at the very end.

  • v10 "Moses" — Mosheh, and Pharaoh's daughter explains it in Hebrew: ki min ha-mayim meshitihu, because I drew him out of the water, from mashah, to draw out. But the form of the name is not passive. Mosheh is an active participle — not the drawn-out one but the one who draws out. She names him for what was done to him and the grammar names him for what he will do.

  • v11 "their burdens" — sivlotam, the word from 1:11, where taskmasters were set over them to afflict them with their burdens. Moses goes out and sees the exact noun the policy was written in.

  • v12 "he turned this way and that, and saw that there was no one around" — va-yifen koh va-khoh. He checks for witnesses before he acts, which tells the reader what he already thinks of the act. And the Hebrew for no one is ein ish, literally no man — the third ish in two verses. He saw an Egyptian man striking a Hebrew man (v11), looked around, and saw no man at all. The next day there turn out to have been witnesses after all.

  • v14 "Who made you a chief and a judge over us?" — the question is meant as an insult and it is also a job description. Forty years later he is exactly that, appointed by someone else. And akhen noda ha-davar, the thing is known — yada, the verb the last chapter used for the king who did not know Joseph.

  • v15 "And he sat down by a well" — the third time in the Bible a man sits at a foreign well and leaves engaged. Abraham's servant met Rebekah at one (Genesis 24), Jacob met Rachel at one (Genesis 29), and the shape repeats here down to the details: a traveler, a well, women with a flock, water drawn, a run home with news, a welcome, a marriage.

  • v17 "and Moses rose and saved them" — va-yoshi'an, from yasha, to save or deliver. It is the root behind the names Joshua and Jesus, and this is the first thing in the Bible Moses does with it — for seven Midianite women he has never met. The same verb reports the sea in 14:30: and the LORD saved Israel that day.

  • v19 "An Egyptian man delivered us" — they take him for an Egyptian, and they are not wrong about how he looks. He was raised in the palace. Two verses later he says his own name for himself: a foreigner in a foreign land.

  • v21 "decided to stay" — vayyo'el, from ya'al, and it is not the ordinary word for deciding. The hiphil of this verb occurs twice in Genesis and once in Exodus, and that is all: Abraham uses it to God at 18:27 and again at 18:31, I have undertaken to speak to my Lord, where it carries the sense of venturing to do something you have no standing to do. Here it is Moses answering an invitation — Reuel had just sent his daughters back for him, call him, and let him eat bread (v20). The man who fled Egypt with nowhere to go says yes to a meal, and the yes turns into a wife, a son, and forty years in Midian.

  • v22 "Gershom" — ger hayiti be-erets nokhriyyah, I have been a foreigner in a foreign land, and the name carries ger in it. A man born a Hebrew, raised an Egyptian, married in Midian, names his son for belonging nowhere.

  • vv23–25 four verbs, and then the sentence stops — God heard their groaning, remembered His covenant, saw the sons of Israel — va-yeda Elohim, and God knew.

    And there the verse ends, with no object. Knew what? The Hebrew does not say, and every English Bible that prints and God took notice of them or and God acknowledged them has supplied something the text withholds. After four hundred years of silence the book says only that God knew, and then changes the subject to a burning bush.

chapters.title: I Will Be What I Will Be
chapters.html:
Exodus 3

1And Moses was shepherding the flock of Jethro his father-in-law, the priest of Midian. And he led the flock to the far side of the wilderness and came to the mountain of God, to Horeb.

2And the messenger of the LORD appeared to him in a flame of fire from the middle of a bush. And he looked, and here — the bush was burning with fire, and the bush was not consumed.

3And Moses said, "Let me turn aside now and see this great sight — why the bush does not burn up."

4And the LORD saw that he had turned aside to see, and God called to him from the middle of the bush and said, "Moses, Moses." And he said, "Here I am."

5And He said, "Do not come near here. Take your sandals off your feet, for the place you are standing on is holy ground."

6And He said, "I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob." And Moses hid his face, for he was afraid to look at God.

I Have Seen, I Have Seen

7And the LORD said, "I have seen, I have seen the affliction of My people who are in Egypt, and I have heard their cry because of their slave drivers, for I know their sufferings.

8And I have come down to rescue them from the hand of Egypt and to bring them up from that land to a good and wide land, to a land flowing with milk and honey — to the place of the Canaanite and the Hittite and the Amorite and the Perizzite and the Hivite and the Jebusite.

9And now, here — the cry of the sons of Israel has come to Me, and I have also seen the crushing with which Egypt is crushing them.

10And now come, and I will send you to Pharaoh, and bring out My people, the sons of Israel, from Egypt."

11And Moses said to God, "Who am I, that I should go to Pharaoh and that I should bring out the sons of Israel from Egypt?"

12And He said, "Because I will be with you. And this is the sign for you that I Myself have sent you: when you bring the people out from Egypt, you will serve God on this mountain."

What Is His Name?

13And Moses said to God, "Here I am, going to the sons of Israel, and I will say to them, 'The God of your fathers has sent me to you,' and they will say to me, 'What is His name?' What shall I say to them?"

14And God said to Moses, "I AM THE ONE WHO WILL BE." And He said, "This is what you shall say to the sons of Israel: I AM has sent me to you."

15And God said further to Moses, "This is what you shall say to the sons of Israel: the LORD, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has sent me to you. This is My name forever, and this is My remembrance for all generations.

16Go and gather the elders of Israel and say to them, 'The LORD, the God of your fathers, appeared to me — the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob — saying: I have surely attended to you and to what is being done to you in Egypt.

17And I have said: I will bring you up out of the affliction of Egypt to the land of the Canaanite and the Hittite and the Amorite and the Perizzite and the Hivite and the Jebusite, to a land flowing with milk and honey.'

18And they will listen to your voice. And you shall come, you and the elders of Israel, to the king of Egypt, and you shall say to him, 'The LORD, the God of the Hebrews, has met with us. And now let us go, please, a three days' journey into the wilderness, and let us sacrifice to the LORD our God.'

19And I Myself know that the king of Egypt will not let you go — not unless by a strong hand.

20And I will stretch out My hand and strike Egypt with all My wonders that I will do in its midst, and after that he will send you out.

21And I will give this people favor in the eyes of Egypt, and it will come to pass that when you go, you will not go empty-handed.

22And every woman will ask of her neighbor and of the woman staying in her house for objects of silver and objects of gold and clothing, and you will put them on your sons and on your daughters — and you will strip Egypt bare."

Notes

  • v1 "to the mountain of God, to Horeb" — the narrator calls it the mountain of God before anything has happened there. Moses is out looking for grazing and walks into a place the storyteller already knows the name of.

  • v2 "a bush" — seneh. Outside this chapter the word appears as a common noun once in the whole Hebrew Bible, in Moses' own blessing at the end of Deuteronomy: the favor of the One who dwells in the bush (Deuteronomy 33:16). And it is one letter from Sinai. The Hebrew never says the two words are related; it just puts God in a seneh on the mountain that becomes Sinai.

  • v2 "the messenger of the LORD" — mal'akh YHWH. The messenger appears in v2 and then is not mentioned again: by v4 it is the LORD who sees and God who calls, out of the same bush. The text slides from one to the other without explaining.

  • v4 "Moses, Moses" — the doubled name is how this book calls someone at the moment everything changes. It happened to Abraham at the binding of Isaac (Genesis 22:11) and to Jacob leaving for Egypt (Genesis 46:2), and both answered exactly as Moses does here: hinneni, here I am.

  • v5 "holy ground" — admat qodesh. Up to this point in the Bible God has made time holy — the seventh day (Genesis 2:3) — but never a place. This is the first holy ground, and it is a patch of wilderness in Midian with a shepherd standing on it, not a temple.

  • v7 "I have seen, I have seen" — ra'oh ra'iti. Hebrew doubles a verb with its own infinitive to press it down hard, and there is no neat English for it. The point is that God is answering the end of chapter 2: God saw, God knew, and now He says so out loud, three times over — seen, heard, known.

  • v8 "a land flowing with milk and honey" — the first of twenty-one times this phrase is used in the Bible, and it is spoken here before Israel has any land at all. Milk means herds that graze, honey means fruit trees. It describes country you can live off without irrigating it — which is to say, the opposite of Egypt.

  • v8 "to rescue them" — le-hatsilo, from natsal. Keep the verb in mind: it comes back in the last verse of the chapter, pointed the other way.

  • v11 "Who am I" — Moses' first objection is not about Pharaoh or the people; it is about himself. He asks who he is. God does not answer the question — the reply in v12 is about who God is.

  • v12 "this is the sign for you... you will serve God on this mountain" — a sign is normally proof given in advance. This one can only be checked after the thing it was supposed to prove has already happened. Moses is being told to go first and find out afterward that he was sent.

  • v14 "I AM THE ONE WHO WILL BE" — ehyeh asher ehyeh, three words built on hayah, to be, and Hebrew has no separate present tense for it: the same word can carry I am, I was, or I will be. The asher in the middle is just who or that — the ordinary word joining clauses everywhere else in the Bible, not a title in itself. Three readings are all defensible: I am who I am (a flat statement of identity), I will be what I will be (open, unfixed), or I will be whatever I choose to be (sovereign self-determination), and nothing in the grammar settles which. This rendering takes both ehyehs at once — the first as am, the second as will be — because that is exactly what the verb leaves open: a name built from a word untouched by tense, spoken by someone claiming to exist before, during, and after everything else. Two verses earlier God told Moses ki ehyeh imakh — I will be with you. The name He gives is the same word as the promise He just made.

  • v15 "the LORD" — the Hebrew here is the four letters YHWH, built from the same verb to be as ehyeh in v14, in the third person: He is or He will be. Jewish practice from antiquity does not pronounce it, and reads Adonai, my Lord, instead — which is why English Bibles print LORD in capitals. Where you see LORD in this rendering, the Hebrew has the four letters.

  • v16 "I have surely attended to you" — paqod paqadti, another doubled verb. It is the exact phrase Joseph used on his deathbed at the end of Genesis: God will surely attend to you and bring you up from this land (Genesis 50:24–25). Joseph said paqod yifqod, He will surely attend. Here God says paqod paqadti, I have surely attended. Same two words, four hundred years later, switched from future to past.

  • v19 "not unless by a strong hand" — the Hebrew is compressed and has been read two ways: that Pharaoh will not let them go even when faced with a strong hand, or that he will not let them go except by one. The difference is whether the strong hand is God's or Pharaoh's, and the words themselves allow both.

  • v22 "you will strip Egypt bare" — ve-nitsaltem et mitsrayim, from natsal, the same verb as rescue in v8. God says He has come down to natsal Israel from Egypt's hand, and closes by saying Israel will natsal Egypt. English needs two different words for it. Hebrew uses one, and the second use is the first one turned around.

speech.text: Exodus 3
And Moses was shepherding the flock of Jethro his father-in-law, the priest of Midian. And he led the flock to the far side of the wilderness and came to the mountain of God, to Horeb.
And the messenger of the LORD appeared to him in a flame of fire from the middle of a bush. And he looked, and here — the bush was burning with fire, and the bush was not consumed.
And Moses said, "Let me turn aside now and see this great sight — why the bush does not burn up."
And the LORD saw that he had turned aside to see, and God called to him from the middle of the bush and said, "Moses, Moses." And he said, "Here I am."
And He said, "Do not come near here. Take your sandals off your feet, for the place you are standing on is holy ground."
And He said, "I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob." And Moses hid his face, for he was afraid to look at God.
I Have Seen, I Have Seen
And the LORD said, "I have seen, I have seen the affliction of My people who are in Egypt, and I have heard their cry because of their slave drivers, for I know their sufferings.

And I have come down to rescue them from the hand of Egypt and to bring them up from that land to a good and wide land, to a land flowing with milk and honey — to the place of the Canaanite and the Hittite and the Amorite and the Perizzite and the Hivite and the Jebusite.
And now, here — the cry of the sons of Israel has come to Me, and I have also seen the crushing with which Egypt is crushing them.
And now come, and I will send you to Pharaoh, and bring out My people, the sons of Israel, from Egypt."
And Moses said to God, "Who am I, that I should go to Pharaoh and that I should bring out the sons of Israel from Egypt?"
And He said, "Because I will be with you. And this is the sign for you that I Myself have sent you: when you bring the people out from Egypt, you will serve God on this mountain."
What Is His Name?

And Moses said to God, "Here I am, going to the sons of Israel, and I will say to them, 'The God of your fathers has sent me to you,' and they will say to me, 'What is His name?' What shall I say to them?"
And God said to Moses, "I AM THE ONE WHO WILL BE." And He said, "This is what you shall say to the sons of Israel: I AM has sent me to you."

And God said further to Moses, "This is what you shall say to the sons of Israel: the LORD, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has sent me to you. This is My name forever, and this is My remembrance for all generations.

Go and gather the elders of Israel and say to them, 'The LORD, the God of your fathers, appeared to me — the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob — saying: I have surely attended to you and to what is being done to you in Egypt.

And I have said: I will bring you up out of the affliction of Egypt to the land of the Canaanite and the Hittite and the Amorite and the Perizzite and the Hivite and the Jebusite, to a land flowing with milk and honey.'

And they will listen to your voice. And you shall come, you and the elders of Israel, to the king of Egypt, and you shall say to him, 'The LORD, the God of the Hebrews, has met with us. And now let us go, please, a three days' journey into the wilderness, and let us sacrifice to the LORD our God.'
And I Myself know that the king of Egypt will not let you go — not unless by a strong hand.
And I will stretch out My hand and strike Egypt with all My wonders that I will do in its midst, and after that he will send you out.
And I will give this people favor in the eyes of Egypt, and it will come to pass that when you go, you will not go empty-handed.

And every woman will ask of her neighbor and of the woman staying in her house for objects of silver and objects of gold and clothing, and you will put them on your sons and on your daughters — and you will strip Egypt bare."

chapters.title: What Is That in Your Hand?
chapters.html:
Exodus 4

1And Moses answered and said, "But look — they will not believe me and will not listen to my voice, for they will say, 'The LORD did not appear to you.'"

2And the LORD said to him, "What is that in your hand?" And he said, "A staff."

3And He said, "Throw it on the ground." And he threw it on the ground, and it became a snake, and Moses ran from it.

4And the LORD said to Moses, "Stretch out your hand and take hold of its tail." And he stretched out his hand and seized it, and it became a staff in his palm —

5"so that they may believe that the LORD, the God of their fathers, appeared to you — the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob."

6And the LORD said to him further, "Put your hand into your cloak." And he put his hand into his cloak, and drew it out, and here — his hand was blighted, white as snow.

7And He said, "Put your hand back into your cloak." And he put his hand back into his cloak and drew it out of his cloak, and here — it had gone back like the rest of his flesh.

8"And it will come to pass, if they do not believe you and do not listen to the voice of the first sign, they will believe the voice of the second sign.

9And it will come to pass, if they do not believe even these two signs and do not listen to your voice, you shall take some of the water of the Nile and pour it on the dry ground, and the water you take from the Nile will become blood on the dry ground."

I Am Heavy of Mouth

10And Moses said to the LORD, "Please, my Lord, I am not a man of words — not yesterday, not the day before, not since You began speaking to Your servant. For I am heavy of mouth and heavy of tongue."

11And the LORD said to him, "Who put a mouth in a man? Or who makes him mute, or deaf, or seeing, or blind? Is it not I, the LORD?

12And now go, and I Myself will be with your mouth, and I will teach you what to say."

13And he said, "Please, my Lord — send someone else."

14And the anger of the LORD burned against Moses, and He said, "Is there not Aaron your brother, the Levite? I know that he can certainly speak. And here — he is even coming out to meet you, and he will see you and be glad in his heart.

15And you shall speak to him and put the words in his mouth, and I Myself will be with your mouth and with his mouth, and I will teach you both what you are to do.

16And he will speak for you to the people, and it will be that he will be a mouth for you, and you will be God for him.

17And you shall take this staff in your hand, with which you will do the signs."

Back to Egypt

18And Moses went and returned to Jether his father-in-law and said to him, "Let me go, please, and return to my brothers who are in Egypt, and see whether they are still alive." And Jethro said to Moses, "Go in peace."

19And the LORD said to Moses in Midian, "Go, return to Egypt, for all the men who were seeking your life are dead."

20And Moses took his wife and his sons and set them on the donkey, and returned to the land of Egypt. And Moses took the staff of God in his hand.

21And the LORD said to Moses, "When you go back to Egypt, see all the wonders I have put in your hand, and do them before Pharaoh. And I Myself will make his heart strong, and he will not send the people away.

22And you shall say to Pharaoh, 'This is what the LORD says: Israel is My son, My firstborn.

23And I said to you, send My son away so he may serve Me, and you refused to send him away. Here — I am killing your son, your firstborn.'"

A Bridegroom of Blood

24And it came to pass on the road, at the lodging place, that the LORD met him and sought to put him to death.

25And Zipporah took a flint and cut off her son's foreskin and touched it to his feet, and said, "A husband of blood you are to me."

26And He let him go. Then she said, "A husband of blood," because of the circumcision.

27And the LORD said to Aaron, "Go to meet Moses in the wilderness." And he went and met him at the mountain of God, and kissed him.

28And Moses told Aaron all the words of the LORD who had sent him, and all the signs He had commanded him.

29And Moses and Aaron went and gathered all the elders of the sons of Israel.

30And Aaron spoke all the words that the LORD had spoken to Moses, and did the signs in the sight of the people.

31And the people believed. And they heard that the LORD had attended to the sons of Israel and that He had seen their affliction, and they bowed down and worshiped.

Notes

  • v2 "What is that in your hand?" — in the written consonants the Hebrew question is a single word, mazzeh; the traditional reading splits it into two, mah zeh, what is this. The scribes preserved both — the letters as written (ketiv) and the words as read aloud (qere) — rather than choosing. Where the two differ, the tradition kept the written text untouched and put the reading in the margin, and English translations are silently picking one of the two.

  • v2 "A staff" — a shepherd's stick, the ordinary tool of the job Moses has been doing for forty years. God does not hand him anything. The whole demonstration is done with what he already brought.

  • v3 "it became a snake" — the sign is not just a wonder; Egypt's crown carries a rearing cobra on the forehead, and Moses is told to grab it by the tail. Handling a snake by the tail is the wrong end, and that appears to be the point.

  • v6 "his hand was blighted, white as snow" — metsora'at, the condition Leviticus 13 legislates, rendered blight there too. English Bibles usually print leprous, but the biblical condition is not the modern disease of that name; it covers a range of skin, fabric, and wall discolorations that make a person or thing unfit to approach the sanctuary. The sign makes Moses untouchable and then undoes it, twice, in two verses.

  • v9 "will become blood on the dry ground" — the third sign is a small private version of what becomes the first plague in 7:20. Here it is a handful of river water poured out in front of the elders.

  • v10 "I am heavy of mouth and heavy of tongue" — kevad peh u-khevad lashon. Heavy, weighted, hard to move. The Hebrew does not name a condition, and it has been read as a stutter, as a speech impairment, and as simple lack of eloquence. What the text says is that his mouth is heavy. The same root kaved is the one used later for Pharaoh's heavy heart.

  • v11 "Who put a mouth in a man?" — Moses says his mouth does not work; God's answer is that He is the one who makes mouths, working and not. It does not fix the mouth. It moves the question.

  • v13 "send someone else" — the Hebrew doubles the verb, shelach... tishlach, "send... you will send." After four objections this is Moses' plain request, and the last thing he says before God gets angry.

  • v14 "the anger of the LORD burned against Moses" — and the anger produces Aaron. The punishment for refusing is that he now has to share the job with his brother. Nothing else happens; God keeps talking in the same breath.

  • v16 "you will be God for him" — ve-attah tihyeh lo le-Elohim. Aaron is the mouth, Moses is the one whose words the mouth carries. The same arrangement is restated in 7:1, where Aaron is called Moses' prophet. It is the clearest working definition of a prophet the Bible gives: not the source of the message, the mouth for it.

  • v18 "Jether his father-in-law" — the name is spelled Yeter in the first half of this verse and Yitro (Jethro) in the second half, in the same sentence. He is also called Reuel in 2:18. The book does not reconcile the names.

  • v20 "the staff of God" — it was a staff in v2, when the question was what Moses had in his hand. Eighteen verses later the narrator calls it the staff of God. The object has not changed.

  • v21 "I Myself will make his heart strong" — va-ani achazzeq et libbo. God says this before Pharaoh has appeared in the story or refused anything. Three different Hebrew verbs are used across the plague accounts for what happens to Pharaoh's heart — chazaq (make strong), kaved (make heavy), qashah (make hard) — and the book distributes them between God doing it and Pharaoh doing it to himself. The first statement of it, here, is God's.

  • v22 "Israel is My son, My firstborn" — the first time God calls the nation His son. It sets up the exchange in the next verse and the last plague at the end of it: a firstborn for a firstborn, announced before a single plague has fallen.

  • vv24–26 "a husband of blood" — three verses, and they are among the most obscure in the Bible. The pronouns are unanchored: the LORD met him and sought to put him to death — Moses or the son, the Hebrew does not say. She touched it to his feet — whose feet, and feet is elsewhere a euphemism. Chatan damim is not a phrase that occurs anywhere else, and chatan specifically names the male relation marriage creates — a groom or son-in-law — not a general word for husband. What is clear is the sequence: God has just called Israel His firstborn son, and immediately a son's blood on a doorpost of flesh turns death aside — which is the Passover, eight chapters early.

  • v31 "the LORD had attended to the sons of Israel" — paqad, the word from 3:16, and from Joseph's deathbed at the end of Genesis. The people believe when they hear it. They have been waiting on that verb for four hundred years.

chapters.title: Who Is the LORD?
chapters.html:
Exodus 5

1And afterward Moses and Aaron came and said to Pharaoh, "This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: Send My people away, and let them hold a feast to Me in the wilderness."

2And Pharaoh said, "Who is the LORD, that I should listen to His voice and send Israel away? I do not know the LORD, and I will not send Israel away either."

3And they said, "The God of the Hebrews has met with us. Let us go, please, a three days' journey into the wilderness and sacrifice to the LORD our God, or He may strike us with plague or with the sword."

4And the king of Egypt said to them, "Moses and Aaron, why are you pulling the people away from their work? Get back to your burdens!"

5And Pharaoh said, "Look — the people of the land are many now, and you would have them rest from their burdens."

Make the Work Heavier

6And that same day Pharaoh commanded the slave drivers of the people and their foremen:

7"You shall not go on giving the people straw to make bricks as before. Let them go and gather straw for themselves.

8And the quota of bricks they were making before, you shall lay on them. You shall not reduce it, because they are slack. That is why they are crying out, saying, 'Let us go and sacrifice to our God.'

9Let the work be heavy on the men, and let them do it, and let them not seek out lies."

10And the slave drivers of the people and their foremen went out and said to the people, "This is what Pharaoh says: I am not giving you straw.

11You go and get straw for yourselves wherever you can find it — because nothing is being reduced from your work."

12And the people scattered through all the land of Egypt to gather stubble for straw.

13And the slave drivers pressed them, saying, "Finish your work — a day's portion by the end of the day, just as when there was straw."

14And the foremen of the sons of Israel, whom Pharaoh's slave drivers had set over them, were beaten, and they were asked, "Why have you not finished your fixed amount of brickmaking, yesterday and today, as you did before?"

Look on Us and Judge

15And the foremen of the sons of Israel came and cried out to Pharaoh, "Why do you do this to your servants?

16No straw is given to your servants, and they say to us, 'Make bricks!' And here — your servants are being beaten, and it is your own people who are at fault."

17And he said, "Slack — you are slack! That is why you say, 'Let us go and sacrifice to the LORD.'

18And now go, work! And straw will not be given to you, and you will hand over the full count of bricks."

19And the foremen of the sons of Israel saw that they were in trouble when they were told, "The day's amount is still required."

20And they met Moses and Aaron, who were standing there to meet them as they came out from Pharaoh.

21And they said to them, "May the LORD look on you and judge, because you have made us stink in the eyes of Pharaoh and in the eyes of his servants — putting a sword in their hand to kill us."

22And Moses went back to the LORD and said, "My Lord, why have You done harm to this people? Why did You ever send me?

23From the moment I came to Pharaoh to speak in Your name, he has done harm to this people — and rescue, You have not rescued Your people."

Notes

  • v2 "I do not know the LORD" — lo yadati. This book keeps turning on that verb. A king arose who did not know Joseph (1:8). God knew (2:25). Moses' killing became known (2:14). Now Pharaoh says the one thing that makes him the enemy: he does not know this name. Everything from here to chapter 14 is God answering it — the phrase that you may know that I am the LORD runs through the plagues like a refrain.

  • v3 "The God of the Hebrews has met with us" — the words God gave Moses at the bush (3:18), repeated verbatim. But look at what the brothers add on their own: or He may strike us with plague or with the sword. God did not say that. They are arguing that letting them go protects Pharaoh's workforce, and they have invented the threat to do it.

  • v4 "pulling the people away" — tafri'u, from para, to let loose or let go slack. It is the verb for undoing restraint. Pharaoh is accusing them of loosening something he has tied down.

  • v4 "your burdens" — sivlotekhem, the word from 1:11 and 2:11, where Moses first went out and saw his brothers' burdens. Pharaoh throws the same noun back at him.

  • v7 "straw to make bricks" — teven and levenim. In Hebrew the two words sound almost the same, and the chapter hammers them together nine times. What is being described is a work order, and it clicks like one.

  • v12 "to gather stubble for straw" — le-qoshesh qash la-teven. They are not given straw, so they gather qash, stubble — the leftovers. The Hebrew even makes the verb and the noun the same sound. They are scavenging chaff to meet a brick quota.

  • v9 "Let the work be heavy" — tikhbad, from kaved, heavy. It is the root already used for Moses' heavy mouth (4:10) and, in the chapters ahead, for Pharaoh's heavy heart. The same weight sits on the slave, the prophet, and the king.

  • v13, 19 "a day's portion by the end of the day" / "the day's amount" — devar yom be-yomo, the same phrase both verses. It is the fixed formula for a daily allotment. Israel will hear it again in the wilderness at 16:4, where the thing measured out daily is not bricks but bread.

  • v16 "it is your own people who are at fault" — the Hebrew of this clause is compressed and has been read two ways: that Pharaoh's own people are the ones in the wrong, or that the fault is being laid on the foremen and so on Pharaoh's people by extension. Chatat is the word for sin or fault, and the sentence does not say clearly whose. The foremen are accusing the crown to its face, and the grammar is as careful as they must have been.

  • v17 "Slack — you are slack!" — nirpim attem nirpim, the word doubled. Pharaoh answers a complaint about beatings by repeating an insult from his own memo (v8). He is not reasoning; he is quoting himself.

  • v21 "you have made us stink" — hiv'ashtem et rechenu, literally you have made our smell stink. It is a physical verb: ba'ash is what the Nile does when the fish die in it (7:18, 7:21) and what the hoarded manna does overnight (16:20). The foremen reach for the ugliest word available.

  • v23 "and rescue, You have not rescued" — ve-hatsel lo hitsalta, the doubled construction Hebrew uses to press a verb down hard. And the verb is natsal — the one God used at the bush: I have come down to rescue them (3:8). Moses ends the chapter by taking God's own word and handing it back empty. The book's first prayer is an accusation.

chapters.title: I Am the LORD
chapters.html:
Exodus 6

1And the LORD said to Moses, "Now you will see what I will do to Pharaoh. For with a strong hand he will send them away, and with a strong hand he will drive them out of his land."

2And God spoke to Moses and said to him, "I am the LORD.

3And I appeared to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob as God Almighty — and by My name, the LORD, I was not known to them.

4And I also established My covenant with them, to give them the land of Canaan, the land where they lived as foreigners.

5And I have also heard the groaning of the sons of Israel, whom the Egyptians are enslaving, and I have remembered My covenant.

6Therefore say to the sons of Israel: I am the LORD. And I will bring you out from under the burdens of Egypt, and I will rescue you from their slavery, and I will redeem you with an outstretched arm and with great acts of judgment.

7And I will take you to Myself as a people, and I will be God to you. And you will know that I am the LORD your God, who brings you out from under the burdens of Egypt.

8And I will bring you to the land that I raised My hand to give to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, and I will give it to you as a possession. I am the LORD."

9And Moses spoke this to the sons of Israel, and they did not listen to Moses, out of shortness of breath and hard slavery.

10And the LORD spoke to Moses:

11"Go, speak to Pharaoh king of Egypt, and let him send the sons of Israel out of his land."

12And Moses spoke before the LORD, "Look — the sons of Israel have not listened to me. How then will Pharaoh listen to me? My lips are still as covered as if they were uncircumcised."

13And the LORD spoke to Moses and to Aaron and gave them a charge concerning the sons of Israel and concerning Pharaoh king of Egypt, to bring the sons of Israel out of the land of Egypt.

These Are the Heads of Their Fathers' Houses

14These are the heads of their fathers' houses. The sons of Reuben, Israel's firstborn: Hanoch and Pallu, Hezron and Carmi. These are the families of Reuben.

15And the sons of Simeon: Jemuel and Jamin and Ohad and Jachin and Zohar, and Shaul the son of the Canaanite woman. These are the families of Simeon.

16And these are the names of the sons of Levi, by their generations: Gershon and Kohath and Merari. And the years of the life of Levi were a hundred and thirty-seven years.

17The sons of Gershon: Libni and Shimei, by their families.

18And the sons of Kohath: Amram and Izhar and Hebron and Uzziel. And the years of the life of Kohath were a hundred and thirty-three years.

19And the sons of Merari: Mahli and Mushi. These are the families of the Levites by their generations.

20And Amram took Jochebed his father's sister as his wife, and she bore him Aaron and Moses. And the years of the life of Amram were a hundred and thirty-seven years.

21And the sons of Izhar: Korah and Nepheg and Zichri.

22And the sons of Uzziel: Mishael and Elzaphan and Sithri.

23And Aaron took Elisheba, daughter of Amminadab, sister of Nahshon, as his wife, and she bore him Nadab and Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar.

24And the sons of Korah: Assir and Elkanah and Abiasaph. These are the families of the Korahites.

25And Eleazar son of Aaron took one of the daughters of Putiel as his wife, and she bore him Phinehas. These are the heads of the fathers' houses of the Levites, by their families.

26This is the Aaron and Moses to whom the LORD said, "Bring the sons of Israel out of the land of Egypt by their divisions."

27They are the ones who spoke to Pharaoh king of Egypt, to bring the sons of Israel out of Egypt. This is the Moses and Aaron.

28And it came to pass on the day the LORD spoke to Moses in the land of Egypt,

29that the LORD spoke to Moses: "I am the LORD. Speak to Pharaoh king of Egypt everything I say to you."

30And Moses said before the LORD, "Look — my lips are still as covered as if they were uncircumcised. How then will Pharaoh listen to me?"

Notes

  • v1 "with a strong hand he will send them away" — be-yad chazakah. At the bush God said Pharaoh would not let them go not unless by a strong hand (3:19), and the Hebrew left it open whose hand that was. Here the sentence reads most naturally as Pharaoh's: the strong hand is on him, and it makes him not merely release them but drive them out. The last plague ends exactly that way.

  • v3 "by My name, the LORD, I was not known to them" — the hardest verse in the chapter, because Genesis contradicts it on its face. God says I am the LORD to Abraham in Genesis 15:7, and Genesis 4:26 says that already in Adam's grandson's day men began to call on the name of the LORD. The Hebrew here is a passive, lo noda'ti, I was not made known — which is not quite the same as saying they never heard the syllables. Readers have taken it three ways: that the name was spoken but its meaning was not yet demonstrated; that the clause is a question — and by My name was I not known to them?; or that the verse comes from a strand of the tradition that told it differently. The Hebrew allows all three. It does not settle it.

  • vv6–7 "I will bring out... rescue... redeem... take" — four promises, each a separate Hebrew verb, each beginning I will: ve-hotseti, ve-hitsalti, ve-ga'alti, ve-laqachti. They are the backbone of the Passover seder, where the four cups are counted off against these four verbs. Whatever the ritual's age, the four are really there, in a row, in this verse.

  • v6 "I will rescue you" — ve-hitsalti, from natsal — the exact verb Moses threw back at God in the last line of chapter 5: and rescue, You have not rescued. God's first word in reply uses it. The two chapters are one conversation.

  • v6 "with an outstretched arm" — bi-zroa netuyah. Egyptian royal art shows the pharaoh with arm raised to strike; the phrase puts that image on someone else. It becomes a fixed expression for the exodus and is still being quoted centuries later.

  • v9 "out of shortness of breath" — mi-qotser ruach. Ruach is breath, wind, spirit. The phrase can mean impatience, or it can mean what it plainly says: people worked past the point of being able to take in a sentence. Given and hard slavery right beside it, the physical reading is the likelier one.

  • v12 "as if they were uncircumcised" — aral sefatayim. In chapter 4 Moses said he was heavy of mouth; now he says something different. Aral is the circumcision word, appearing two chapters after Zipporah's flint knife — the same word used of fruit not yet fit to eat in Leviticus 19:23. It marks something closed off, not yet fit for use. He is not repeating the old complaint. He has found a worse one.

  • vv14–25 the genealogy stops at Levi — it begins dutifully with Reuben and Simeon, the first two sons, and then reaches Levi, the third, and simply stays there. Everyone after that is Levi's line. The list is not a census; it exists to place Moses and Aaron, and it abandons the other nine tribes the moment it has done so.

  • v20 "Amram took Jochebed his father's sister" — his aunt. Leviticus 18:12 forbids exactly this: you shall not uncover the nakedness of your father's sister. The text records the parentage of Moses without comment, and the law that would later prohibit it is in the same five books.

  • v23 "Elisheba, daughter of Amminadab, sister of Nahshon" — Aaron's wife is given three identifiers where most wives here get none. Nahshon is the chief of Judah, and the line runs to David. The priesthood and the kingship are married into each other in one verse.

  • v26 "This is the Aaron and Moses"... v27 "This is the Moses and Aaron" — the names are given in one order, then the other, in consecutive verses. The Hebrew is deliberate: the speaking is credited to them jointly, and the text refuses to settle which brother goes first.

  • v30 repeats v12 — the genealogy interrupts a conversation, and when it ends, the text picks the conversation up by restating Moses' objection word for word. The seam is visible, and nobody smoothed it.

chapters.title: All the Water Turned to Blood
chapters.html:
Exodus 7

1And the LORD said to Moses, "See, I have made you God to Pharaoh, and Aaron your brother will be your prophet.

2You shall speak everything I command you, and Aaron your brother shall speak to Pharaoh, so that he sends the sons of Israel out of his land.

3And I Myself will make Pharaoh's heart hard, and I will multiply My signs and My wonders in the land of Egypt.

4And Pharaoh will not listen to you, and I will set My hand against Egypt, and I will bring out My divisions, My people the sons of Israel, from the land of Egypt with great acts of judgment.

5And Egypt will know that I am the LORD, when I stretch out My hand against Egypt and bring the sons of Israel out from among them."

6And Moses and Aaron did as the LORD commanded them — so they did.

7And Moses was eighty years old and Aaron eighty-three years old when they spoke to Pharaoh.

The Staff That Swallowed the Staffs

8And the LORD said to Moses and to Aaron:

9"When Pharaoh says to you, 'Produce a wonder for yourselves,' then say to Aaron, 'Take your staff and throw it down before Pharaoh' — and it will become a serpent."

10And Moses and Aaron came to Pharaoh and did so, as the LORD had commanded. And Aaron threw down his staff before Pharaoh and before his servants, and it became a serpent.

11And Pharaoh also called for the wise men and the sorcerers, and they too — the magicians of Egypt — did the same with their secret arts.

12And each one threw down his staff, and they became serpents. And Aaron's staff swallowed their staffs.

13And Pharaoh's heart was strong, and he did not listen to them, just as the LORD had said.

The First Blow

14And the LORD said to Moses, "Pharaoh's heart is heavy. He refuses to send the people away.

15Go to Pharaoh in the morning — look, he is going out to the water — and stand to meet him on the bank of the Nile. And take in your hand the staff that turned into a snake.

16And say to him, 'The LORD, the God of the Hebrews, sent me to you, saying: Send My people away, so they may serve Me in the wilderness. And here — you have not listened, until now.

17This is what the LORD says: By this you will know that I am the LORD. Here — I am striking the water that is in the Nile with the staff that is in my hand, and it will turn to blood.

18And the fish that are in the Nile will die, and the Nile will stink, and Egypt will be unable to drink water from the Nile.'"

19And the LORD said to Moses, "Say to Aaron: Take your staff and stretch out your hand over the waters of Egypt — over their rivers, over their canals, over their pools, and over every gathering of their water — and they will become blood. And there will be blood in all the land of Egypt, even in the wooden and the stone vessels."

20And Moses and Aaron did so, as the LORD commanded. And he raised the staff and struck the water that was in the Nile, before the eyes of Pharaoh and before the eyes of his servants, and all the water in the Nile turned to blood.

21And the fish that were in the Nile died, and the Nile stank, and Egypt could not drink water from the Nile. And the blood was in all the land of Egypt.

22And the magicians of Egypt did the same with their secret arts, and Pharaoh's heart was strong, and he did not listen to them, just as the LORD had said.

23And Pharaoh turned and went into his house, and he did not set his heart to this either.

24And all Egypt dug around the Nile for water to drink, because they could not drink from the water of the Nile.

25And seven days were filled after the LORD struck the Nile.

Notes

  • v1 "I have made you God to Pharaoh, and Aaron your brother will be your prophet" — the plainest definition of a prophet the Bible gives, and it is given as a job description rather than a doctrine. A prophet is not the source of the message. He is the mouth for it. The arrangement was set up in 4:16, where Aaron is a mouth for you and Moses is God for him; here the second word, navi, prophet, is supplied.

  • v3 "I will make Pharaoh's heart hard" — aqsheh, from qashah, to be hard or stiff. This is the third Hebrew verb for what happens to Pharaoh's heart, and all three appear within eleven verses of each other: qashah here, hard; chazaq in v13, strong; kaved in v14, heavy. English flattens all three into hardened. The Hebrew keeps them apart, and it also keeps track of who does it — God hardens in v3, and in v13 and v22 the heart simply was strong, with no one named.

  • v9 "a serpent" — tannin, and this is not the word from chapter 4. There the staff became a nachash, an ordinary snake. Here it becomes a tannin — the word for a sea-monster, a great reptile, the creature God makes on the fifth day of creation in Genesis 1:21. The sign has been upgraded for the throne room. Then in v15 the narrator refers back to it as the staff that turned into a nachash, using the smaller word again. The text does not harmonize itself.

  • v11 "with their secret arts" — the Hebrew word here is belahatehem, built on lahat, flame or blade. Eleven verses later, at v22, the same phrase is spelled belatehem, built on lat, secrecy or concealment. One letter apart, two different pictures — flashing and hiding — and the chapter uses both.

  • v11 "the magicians of Egypt" — chartummim, a loanword from Egyptian rather than a Hebrew coinage. The narrator uses the Egyptians' own professional title. They are not frauds in this account: they do what Aaron does.

  • v12 "Aaron's staff swallowed their staffs" — va-yivla, from bala, to swallow. Egypt's magic is not shown to be false; it is shown to be eaten. The same verb returns in the song after the sea: You stretched out Your right hand — the earth swallowed them (15:12).

  • v17 "By this you will know that I am the LORD" — the answer to Pharaoh's question in 5:2, Who is the LORD? I do not know the LORD. He asked to be introduced. The plagues are the introduction, and this sentence is its formula — it recurs through the whole sequence.

  • v19 "even in the wooden and the stone vessels" — the blow does not stop at the river. It reaches the water already drawn and standing in the house. Egypt's life is organised around the Nile, and the first plague follows that organisation indoors.

  • v18 "the Nile will stink" — u-va'ash, the same verb the Israelite foremen used against Moses two chapters earlier: you have made us stink in the eyes of Pharaoh (5:21). What they accused him of doing to them, the Nile now does in fact.

  • v23 "he did not set his heart to this either" — lo shat libbo gam la-zot. Not defiance; indifference. He went home. The word either is doing real work: the text is counting, and it expects the reader to notice that this has now happened more than once.

  • v25 "seven days were filled" — the only interval given in the plague sequence. The narrative almost never tells you how long anything lasts, and here it stops to say a week passed with the river undrinkable before anything else happened.

chapters.title: The Finger of God
chapters.html:
Exodus 8

1And the LORD said to Moses, "Go to Pharaoh and say to him, 'This is what the LORD says: Send My people away, so they may serve Me.

2And if you refuse to send them away, here — I am striking your whole territory with frogs.

3And the Nile will swarm with frogs, and they will come up and come into your house, and into your bedroom, and onto your bed, and into the house of your servants, and among your people, and into your ovens and into your kneading bowls.

4And on you and on your people and on all your servants the frogs will come up.'"

5And the LORD said to Moses, "Say to Aaron: Stretch out your hand with your staff over the rivers, over the canals, and over the pools, and bring the frogs up over the land of Egypt."

6And Aaron stretched out his hand over the waters of Egypt, and the frog came up and covered the land of Egypt.

7And the magicians did the same with their secret arts, and they brought frogs up over the land of Egypt.

8And Pharaoh called for Moses and Aaron and said, "Plead with the LORD to take the frogs away from me and from my people, and I will send the people away, and they will sacrifice to the LORD."

9And Moses said to Pharaoh, "Claim the honor over me: for when shall I plead for you and for your servants and for your people, to cut off the frogs from you and from your houses, so that they are left only in the Nile?"

10And he said, "Tomorrow." And he said, "As you say — so that you may know that there is none like the LORD our God.

11And the frogs will turn aside from you and from your houses and from your servants and from your people. They will be left only in the Nile."

12And Moses and Aaron went out from Pharaoh, and Moses cried out to the LORD about the matter of the frogs that He had set on Pharaoh.

13And the LORD did according to Moses' word, and the frogs died out of the houses, out of the courtyards, and out of the fields.

14And they piled them up, heap after heap, and the land stank.

15And Pharaoh saw that there was relief, and he made his own heart heavy, and he did not listen to them, just as the LORD had said.

The Finger of God

16And the LORD said to Moses, "Say to Aaron: Stretch out your staff and strike the dust of the earth, and it will become gnats in all the land of Egypt."

17And they did so. And Aaron stretched out his hand with his staff and struck the dust of the earth, and the gnats were on man and on beast. All the dust of the earth became gnats in all the land of Egypt.

18And the magicians did the same with their secret arts, to bring out the gnats — and they could not. And the gnats were on man and on beast.

19And the magicians said to Pharaoh, "This is the finger of God." And Pharaoh's heart was strong, and he did not listen to them, just as the LORD had said.

A Separation Between My People and Your People

20And the LORD said to Moses, "Rise early in the morning and station yourself before Pharaoh — look, he is going out to the water — and say to him, 'This is what the LORD says: Send My people away, so they may serve Me.

21For if you are not sending My people away, here — I am letting loose against you and against your servants and against your people and against your houses the swarms. And the houses of Egypt will be full of the swarms, and also the ground they stand on.

22And on that day I will set apart the land of Goshen, where My people are standing, so that no swarms are there — so that you may know that I am the LORD in the midst of the land.

23And I will put a ransom between My people and your people. Tomorrow this sign will happen.'"

24And the LORD did so, and heavy swarms came into Pharaoh's house and the house of his servants, and in all the land of Egypt the land was ruined because of the swarms.

25And Pharaoh called for Moses and Aaron and said, "Go, sacrifice to your God — in the land."

26And Moses said, "It would not be right to do so, because what we sacrifice to the LORD our God is detestable to Egypt. If we sacrifice what is detestable to Egypt before their eyes, will they not stone us?

27A three days' journey we will go into the wilderness, and we will sacrifice to the LORD our God as He tells us."

28And Pharaoh said, "I myself will send you away, and you will sacrifice to the LORD your God in the wilderness — only you shall not go very far away. Plead for me."

29And Moses said, "Here — I am going out from you, and I will plead with the LORD, and the swarms will turn aside from Pharaoh, from his servants, and from his people tomorrow. Only let Pharaoh not go on trifling, by not sending the people away to sacrifice to the LORD."

30And Moses went out from Pharaoh and pleaded with the LORD.

31And the LORD did according to Moses' word, and He took the swarms away from Pharaoh, from his servants, and from his people. Not one was left.

32And Pharaoh made his heart heavy this time too, and he did not send the people away.

Notes

  • On the verse numbers — the Hebrew text divides these chapters differently: what is printed here as 8:1–4 stands in the Hebrew as 7:26–29, so the Hebrew chapter 8 runs to 28 verses and this one to 32. This rendering follows the English division, so a reader can set it beside a King James Bible. Nothing of the text is added or lost either way.

  • v3 "the Nile will swarm with frogs" — ve-sharats ha-ye'or. Sharats is the swarming verb of the fifth day of creation — let the waters swarm with swarms of living creatures (Genesis 1:20) — and it is one of the five verbs used of Israel multiplying in Egypt in Exodus 1:7. The Nile was where Hebrew boys were drowned. Now the same river swarms, and what comes out of it goes into Pharaoh's bed.

  • v3 "into your ovens and into your kneading bowls" — the plague is aimed at the places a household cannot do without. Bread cannot be made. What the text lists is not horror but the shutting down of ordinary domestic life, item by item.

  • v6 "and the frog came up and covered the land" — the Hebrew noun is singular: va-ta'al ha-tsefardea, and the frog came up. Hebrew can use a singular collectively, so this is grammar rather than a single enormous animal, but the effect is not lost on the reader who sees it — one creature, covering Egypt.

  • v9 "Claim the honor over me" — hitpa'er alai, an odd idiom built on pa'ar, to glorify or beautify. Moses is handing Pharaoh the advantage: you name the hour. It is a piece of courtesy with a hook in it, and it sets up what Pharaoh does next.

  • v10 "Tomorrow" — offered any moment he likes, Pharaoh picks the day after. He chooses one more night in a house full of frogs rather than be relieved on someone else's schedule. The text reports the word and says nothing about it.

  • v14 "heap after heap, and the land stank" — chomarim chomarim, the noun doubled, which is how Hebrew says piles and piles. And va-tiv'ash, the stink verb again — the Nile stank in 7:21, the foremen said Moses made them stink in 5:21. Relief, in this chapter, smells worse than the plague.

  • v15 "he made his own heart heavy" — ve-hakhbed et libbo. Up to here the heart has been strong (7:13, 7:22) or God has said He would harden it (7:3). This is the first time Pharaoh does it to himself, and the Hebrew is an emphatic form that puts the act squarely on him. He does it again in the last verse of the chapter.

  • v17 "the dust of the earth" — afar ha-arets, the stuff man was formed from in Genesis 2:7. Aaron strikes it and it becomes vermin. The previous sign struck water; this one strikes the ground itself.

  • v18 "to bring out the gnats — and they could not" — le-hotsi, the same verb used throughout this book for bringing Israel out of Egypt. The magicians attempt a bringing-out and fail at it. It is the first thing in the contest that Egypt cannot do.

  • v19 "This is the finger of God" — etsba Elohim hi. Egypt's own experts say it, not Moses, and they say Elohim, God, rather than the name. It is the first concession from the other side, and Pharaoh ignores his own advisers. The same phrase returns for the writing of the tablets at 31:18.

  • v21 "the swarms" — he-arov, from a root meaning to mix. The word says a mixture, not which creatures, and ancient readers already disagreed: some took it as flies, others as a mixed mass of wild animals. The Hebrew declines to specify, and this rendering keeps it unspecified.

  • v23 "I will put a ransom between My people and your people" — pedut, and this is not the ordinary word for a division or a boundary. Pedut means a ransom, a redemption, the price paid to get someone back. Some read it here as a sign of deliverance, others emend it toward a word for distinction. What the received text says is that what stands between the two peoples is a ransom.

  • v26 "what we sacrifice is detestable to Egypt" — to'evat mitsrayim, and Genesis has used that exact phrase twice about these two peoples: Egyptians could not eat bread with Hebrews, for that is detestable to Egypt (43:32), and every shepherd is detestable to Egypt (46:34). Moses is not inventing an excuse; he is quoting a fact the book established four hundred years earlier.

  • v28 "only you shall not go very far away" — the Hebrew doubles the verb, harcheq lo tarchiqu, distancing you shall not distance. Pharaoh has moved from no to haggling over mileage. It is the first concession, and it is about geography rather than freedom.

  • v29 "let Pharaoh not go on trifling" — hatel, to mock, to deal falsely, to play someone. Moses says it to the king's face, and the last verse of the chapter proves him right.
