And on you and on your people and on all your servants the frogs will come up.'"
And the LORD said to Moses, "Say to Aaron: Stretch out your hand with your staff over the rivers, over the canals, and over the pools, and bring the frogs up over the land of Egypt."
And Aaron stretched out his hand over the waters of Egypt, and the frog came up and covered the land of Egypt.
And the magicians did the same with their secret arts, and they brought frogs up over the land of Egypt.
And Pharaoh called for Moses and Aaron and said, "Plead with the LORD to take the frogs away from me and from my people, and I will send the people away, and they will sacrifice to the LORD."

And Moses said to Pharaoh, "Claim the honor over me: for when shall I plead for you and for your servants and for your people, to cut off the frogs from you and from your houses, so that they are left only in the Nile?"
And he said, "Tomorrow." And he said, "As you say — so that you may know that there is none like the LORD our God.
And the frogs will turn aside from you and from your houses and from your servants and from your people. They will be left only in the Nile."
And Moses and Aaron went out from Pharaoh, and Moses cried out to the LORD about the matter of the frogs that He had set on Pharaoh.
And the LORD did according to Moses' word, and the frogs died out of the houses, out of the courtyards, and out of the fields.
And they piled them up, heap after heap, and the land stank.
And Pharaoh saw that there was relief, and he made his own heart heavy, and he did not listen to them, just as the LORD had said.
The Finger of God
And the LORD said to Moses, "Say to Aaron: Stretch out your staff and strike the dust of the earth, and it will become gnats in all the land of Egypt."

And they did so. And Aaron stretched out his hand with his staff and struck the dust of the earth, and the gnats were on man and on beast. All the dust of the earth became gnats in all the land of Egypt.
And the magicians did the same with their secret arts, to bring out the gnats — and they could not. And the gnats were on man and on beast.
And the magicians said to Pharaoh, "This is the finger of God." And Pharaoh's heart was strong, and he did not listen to them, just as the LORD had said.
A Separation Between My People and Your People

And the LORD said to Moses, "Rise early in the morning and station yourself before Pharaoh — look, he is going out to the water — and say to him, 'This is what the LORD says: Send My people away, so they may serve Me.

For if you are not sending My people away, here — I am letting loose against you and against your servants and against your people and against your houses the swarms. And the houses of Egypt will be full of the swarms, and also the ground they stand on.
And on that day I will set apart the land of Goshen, where My people are standing, so that no swarms are there — so that you may know that I am the LORD in the midst of the land.
And I will put a ransom between My people and your people. Tomorrow this sign will happen.'"
And the LORD did so, and heavy swarms came into Pharaoh's house and the house of his servants, and in all the land of Egypt the land was ruined because of the swarms.
And Pharaoh called for Moses and Aaron and said, "Go, sacrifice to your God — in the land."

And Moses said, "It would not be right to do so, because what we sacrifice to the LORD our God is detestable to Egypt. If we sacrifice what is detestable to Egypt before their eyes, will they not stone us?
A three days' journey we will go into the wilderness, and we will sacrifice to the LORD our God as He tells us."
And Pharaoh said, "I myself will send you away, and you will sacrifice to the LORD your God in the wilderness — only you shall not go very far away. Plead for me."

And Moses said, "Here — I am going out from you, and I will plead with the LORD, and the swarms will turn aside from Pharaoh, from his servants, and from his people tomorrow. Only let Pharaoh not go on trifling, by not sending the people away to sacrifice to the LORD."
And Moses went out from Pharaoh and pleaded with the LORD.
And the LORD did according to Moses' word, and He took the swarms away from Pharaoh, from his servants, and from his people. Not one was left.
And Pharaoh made his heart heavy this time too, and he did not send the people away.

chapters.title: I Have Sinned This Time
chapters.html:
Exodus 9

1And the LORD said to Moses, "Go to Pharaoh and speak to him: This is what the LORD, the God of the Hebrews, says: Send My people away, so they may serve Me.

2For if you refuse to send them away, and you go on holding them,

3here — the hand of the LORD is coming against your livestock that are in the field: against the horses, the donkeys, the camels, the herd and the flock — a very heavy plague.

4And the LORD will make a distinction between the livestock of Israel and the livestock of Egypt, and not one thing belonging to the sons of Israel will die."

5And the LORD set an appointed time, saying, "Tomorrow the LORD will do this thing in the land."

6And the LORD did this thing the next day, and all the livestock of Egypt died, and of the livestock of the sons of Israel not one died.

7And Pharaoh sent, and here — not so much as one of Israel's livestock had died. And Pharaoh's heart was heavy, and he did not send the people away.

Soot from the Kiln

8And the LORD said to Moses and to Aaron, "Take for yourselves handfuls of soot from a kiln, and let Moses throw it toward the sky before the eyes of Pharaoh.

9And it will become fine dust over all the land of Egypt, and it will become boils breaking out in blisters on man and on beast in all the land of Egypt."

10And they took the soot of the kiln and stood before Pharaoh, and Moses threw it toward the sky, and it became boils, blisters breaking out on man and on beast.

11And the magicians could not stand before Moses because of the boils, for the boils were on the magicians and on all Egypt.

12And the LORD made Pharaoh's heart strong, and he did not listen to them, just as the LORD had said to Moses.

Hail and Fire

13And the LORD said to Moses, "Rise early in the morning and station yourself before Pharaoh and say to him: This is what the LORD, the God of the Hebrews, says: Send My people away, so they may serve Me.

14For this time I am sending all My blows to your heart, and against your servants and against your people — so that you may know that there is none like Me in all the earth.

15For by now I could have stretched out My hand and struck you and your people with plague, and you would have been wiped from the earth.

16But for this very reason I have kept you standing: to show you My power, and so that My name may be told in all the earth.

17You are still lording it over My people, refusing to send them away.

18Here — about this time tomorrow I am raining down very heavy hail, such as there has never been in Egypt from the day it was founded until now.

19And now, send word — bring your livestock into shelter, and everything you have in the field. Every man and beast found in the field and not gathered into the house — the hail will come down on them and they will die."

20Whoever among Pharaoh's servants feared the word of the LORD made his servants and his livestock flee into the houses.

21And whoever did not set his heart to the word of the LORD left his servants and his livestock in the field.

22And the LORD said to Moses, "Stretch out your hand toward the sky, and there will be hail in all the land of Egypt — on man and on beast and on every plant of the field in the land of Egypt."

23And Moses stretched out his staff toward the sky, and the LORD gave thunder and hail, and fire went down to the earth. And the LORD rained hail on the land of Egypt.

24And there was hail, and fire flashing in the middle of the hail, very heavy — such as there had never been in all the land of Egypt since it became a nation.

25And the hail struck, in all the land of Egypt, everything that was in the field, from man to beast. And the hail struck every plant of the field and shattered every tree of the field.

26Only in the land of Goshen, where the sons of Israel were, there was no hail.

The LORD Is the Righteous One

27And Pharaoh sent and called for Moses and Aaron and said to them, "I have sinned this time. The LORD is the righteous one, and I and my people are the guilty ones.

28Plead with the LORD — there has been enough of God's thunder and hail — and I will send you away, and you will not go on standing here."

29And Moses said to him, "As I go out of the city I will spread out my hands to the LORD. The thunder will stop and the hail will be no more, so that you may know that the earth belongs to the LORD.

30But as for you and your servants, I know that you do not yet fear the LORD God."

31And the flax and the barley were struck, because the barley was in the ear and the flax was in bud.

32And the wheat and the spelt were not struck, because they are late.

33And Moses went out of the city, away from Pharaoh, and spread out his hands to the LORD, and the thunder and the hail stopped, and rain no longer poured on the earth.

34And Pharaoh saw that the rain and the hail and the thunder had stopped, and he went on sinning, and he made his heart heavy — he and his servants.

35And Pharaoh's heart was strong, and he did not send the sons of Israel away, just as the LORD had said through Moses.

Notes

  • v3 "the hand of the LORD is coming" — the Hebrew word is hoyah, a participle built on hayah, to be, and this spelling of it occurs nowhere else in the Bible. It is the verb behind the name given at the bush. What is announced as coming against the herds is, in the letters, a form of I will be.

  • v3 "a very heavy plague" — kaved me'od. Watch where the weight goes in this chapter: a heavy plague here, heavy hail in v18 and v24, and Pharaoh's heavy heart in v7 and v34. The same adjective is on the man and on the weather.

  • v6 "all the livestock of Egypt died" — and then there are Egyptian livestock again in v19, and horses at the sea in chapter 14. The Hebrew kol need not be exhaustive, and v3 had already limited the plague to the animals in the field. Still, the sentence as written says all, and the tension is in the text rather than in the translation.

  • v8 "soot from a kiln" — piach kivshan. The kivshan is the furnace where bricks are fired. Israel has been making bricks since chapter 1 and scrounging stubble to fire them since chapter 5. Moses takes a handful of the waste from that process and throws it in the air, and it settles on Egypt as a disease. The instrument of the slavery becomes the plague.

  • v11 "the magicians could not stand before Moses" — their second defeat, and worse than the first. At the gnats they could not perform (8:18). Now they cannot even be in the room. The professionals who opened the contest by matching Aaron staff for staff are written out of it here and never appear again.

  • v12 "the LORD made Pharaoh's heart strong" — the first time in the book that God is stated as the one doing it. Up to now the text has said only that the heart was strong (7:13, 7:22, 8:19) or was heavy (9:7), with no subject named, or has said outright that Pharaoh did it himself (8:15, 8:32). God announced in 7:3 that He would. This verse is where He is finally the grammatical subject of the act — after five refusals Pharaoh made on his own.

  • v16 "I have kept you standing" — he'emadtikha, from amad, to stand. Not raised you up in the sense of creating a man for a purpose, but kept you in place — left you on your feet. Paul quotes this verse in Romans 9:17 and builds an argument about election on it; the Greek he quotes uses a stronger verb, exēgeira, I raised you up.

  • v17 "you are still lording it over My people" — mistolel, and this word appears nowhere else in the Bible. It is built on a root for a raised road or heaped-up embankment, so the sense is something like making yourself high against. Its precise force is unrecoverable; the shape of it is clear enough.

  • v23 "the LORD gave thunder" — Hebrew has no separate word for thunder. It says qolot, voices. So what the LORD gives is voices, and Pharaoh in v28 asks for an end to the voices of God. English has to choose one or the other; the Hebrew hears them as the same thing.

  • v24 "fire flashing in the middle of the hail" — mitlaqachat, a reflexive form: fire taking hold of itself. Ice and fire in one weather system, and the Hebrew describes the fire as self-feeding inside it.

  • v27 "I have sinned this time. The LORD is the righteous one" — the fullest confession any Egyptian makes, and it uses the legal vocabulary exactly: tsaddiq is the one in the right in a dispute, resha'im the ones in the wrong. Pharaoh concedes the verdict. Six verses later he reverses it, and the text notes that his servants joined him this time.

  • vv31–32 "the barley was in the ear and the flax was in bud" — a farmer's aside, and the only thing in the plague sequence that dates it. Barley heads out and flax buds in the same few weeks; wheat and spelt ripen later and were still low enough to survive. The detail also names the season: the barley is aviv, and aviv is what the month of the exodus is called in 13:4.

  • v34 "he and his servants" — the first time the hardening is plural. In v20 some of Pharaoh's servants had feared the word of the LORD and brought their animals in. By the end of the chapter that distinction has closed, and the court is with him.

chapters.title: A Darkness That Can Be Felt
chapters.html:
Exodus 10

1And the LORD said to Moses, "Go to Pharaoh, for I Myself have made his heart heavy and the heart of his servants, so that I may set these signs of Mine among them,

2and so that you may tell in the ears of your son and your son's son what I did in Egypt, and My signs that I set among them — and you will know that I am the LORD."

3And Moses and Aaron came to Pharaoh and said to him, "This is what the LORD, the God of the Hebrews, says: How long will you refuse to humble yourself before Me? Send My people away, so they may serve Me.

4For if you refuse to send My people away, here — tomorrow I am bringing locusts into your territory.

5And they will cover the eye of the land, and no one will be able to see the land. And they will eat what is left of what escaped — what the hail left you — and they will eat every tree that is growing for you out of the field.

6And your houses will be full, and the houses of all your servants and the houses of all Egypt — such as your fathers and your fathers' fathers have not seen, from the day they were on the ground until this day." And he turned and went out from Pharaoh.

7And Pharaoh's servants said to him, "How long will this man be a snare to us? Send the men away, and let them serve the LORD their God. Do you not yet know that Egypt is destroyed?"

8And Moses and Aaron were brought back to Pharaoh, and he said to them, "Go, serve the LORD your God. Who and who are going?"

9And Moses said, "With our young and with our old we will go. With our sons and with our daughters, with our flocks and with our herds we will go, because it is a feast of the LORD for us."

10And he said to them, "May the LORD be with you the way I send you and your little ones away! Look — you have evil in front of your faces.

11Not so. Go, the men among you, and serve the LORD — that is what you are asking for." And he drove them out from Pharaoh's presence.

The Locusts

12And the LORD said to Moses, "Stretch out your hand over the land of Egypt for the locusts, and let them come up over the land of Egypt and eat every plant of the land, everything the hail left."

13And Moses stretched out his staff over the land of Egypt, and the LORD drove an east wind through the land all that day and all that night. Morning came, and the east wind had carried the locusts.

14And the locusts came up over all the land of Egypt and settled in all the territory of Egypt — very heavy. Before them there had never been locusts like them, and after them there will not be.

15And they covered the eye of the whole land, and the land went dark. And they ate every plant of the land and all the fruit of the tree that the hail had left, and nothing green was left on the tree or on the plants of the field in all the land of Egypt.

16And Pharaoh hurried to call for Moses and Aaron and said, "I have sinned against the LORD your God and against you.

17And now, lift my sin just this once, and plead with the LORD your God, and let Him only take this death away from me."

18And he went out from Pharaoh and pleaded with the LORD.

19And the LORD turned the wind around — a very strong sea wind — and it carried the locusts and drove them into the Sea of Reeds. Not one locust was left in all the territory of Egypt.

20And the LORD made Pharaoh's heart strong, and he did not send the sons of Israel away.

Darkness

21And the LORD said to Moses, "Stretch out your hand toward the sky, and there will be darkness over the land of Egypt — and the darkness will be felt."

22And Moses stretched out his hand toward the sky, and there was thick darkness in all the land of Egypt for three days.

23No one saw his brother, and no one got up from where he was for three days. But for all the sons of Israel there was light in their dwellings.

24And Pharaoh called to Moses and said, "Go, serve the LORD. Only your flocks and your herds are to be left behind. Your little ones may go with you too."

25And Moses said, "You yourself must also put sacrifices and burnt offerings in our hands, and we will make them for the LORD our God.

26And our livestock will go with us too — not a hoof will be left behind — because we will take from them to serve the LORD our God, and we do not know how we are to serve the LORD until we get there."

27And the LORD made Pharaoh's heart strong, and he was not willing to send them away.

28And Pharaoh said to him, "Get away from me! Watch yourself — do not see my face again, because on the day you see my face you will die."

29And Moses said, "You have spoken rightly. I will not see your face again."

Notes

  • v1 "I Myself have made his heart heavy and the heart of his servants" — God states it outright, and includes the court. The narrator had already reported the plural at 9:34, where Pharaoh made his heart heavy he and his servants. Both accounts are in the book; neither is dropped.

  • v2 "what I did in Egypt" — the Hebrew verb is hit'allalti, from alal, and it is not a neutral word. It means to deal harshly with, to make a mockery of, to toy with someone. English translations soften it, and the softening is understandable, but the verb the text chose is the one you would use of a stronger party having its way with a weaker one.

  • v2 "tell in the ears of your son and your son's son" — the first command in the book to tell the story, and it arrives before the story has finished happening. The plagues are being staged, the text says here, partly so there will be something to recite. Everything the Passover liturgy later does is authorised by this verse.

  • v3 "refuse to humble yourself" — le'anot, from anah, to be bowed down or afflicted. It is the root of oni, the affliction God says He has seen in 3:7. Pharaoh is being asked to accept the very thing he has been imposing, in the same word.

  • v5 "they will cover the eye of the land" — ein ha-arets, the eye of the land. Hebrew uses ayin for the visible surface of a thing. The idiom does double work here, because what the locusts take away is precisely the ability to see the ground.

  • v7 "How long will this man be a snare to us?" — Pharaoh's own officials turn first, and the word they use, moqesh, is a bird trap. Then: Do you not yet know that Egypt is destroyed? They use the same not yet Moses used to the king's face in 9:30. The court has begun speaking Moses' language.

  • v8 "Who and who are going?" — mi va-mi, the interrogative doubled. It is blunt, almost rude, and it is the sound of a negotiation being reopened on worse terms.

  • v10 "you have evil in front of your faces" — the Hebrew is short and menacing, and it will not resolve. Ra'ah means evil or harm; it can be a warning about what lies ahead of them, an accusation about what they intend, or a threat about what he will do. All three readings fit the words.

  • v11 "and he drove them out" — va-yegaresh, and this is the verb from 6:1, where God said Pharaoh would drive them out of his land with a strong hand. Pharaoh performs the word here in miniature, on two men, thinking he is winning.

  • v13 "an east wind... all that day and all that night" — ruach qadim. Hold this one: at the sea in 14:21 the LORD drives the water back with a strong east wind all night — the same wind, the same duration, the same word. The wind that brings the locusts in is the wind that opens the sea.

  • v19 "a very strong sea wind... into the Sea of Reeds" — and then the wind reverses and dumps the locusts in Yam Suf. The place where Egypt's army will drown is named here first, and what drowns in it first is insects.

  • v15 "the land went dark" — va-techshakh ha-arets. The locusts blacken the sky, and that is the last thing the ninth plague needs; the next one simply removes the light. The text moves from a darkness made of bodies to a darkness made of nothing.

  • v21 "the darkness will be felt" — ve-yamesh choshekh, from a root for groping with the hands. Darkness thick enough to touch. And choshekh is the word lying on the face of the deep in Genesis 1:2, before God says let there be light. The plague is a piece of the world put back the way it was before the first day.

  • v23 "no one got up from where he was" — three days without seeing a face, without standing up. It is the only plague with no physical damage at all: nothing is killed, nothing is eaten, nothing is broken. Egypt is simply stopped.

  • v26 "not a hoof will be left behind" — lo tisha'er parsah. Pharaoh has been bargaining piece by piece — the men only, then the children too, now everything but the animals. Moses answers with the smallest unit he can name.

  • v26 "we do not know how we are to serve the LORD until we get there" — the honest sentence in the middle of the argument. Moses is not withholding a plan. There is no plan yet. The instructions for worship do not exist until Sinai.

And Pharaoh said to him, "Get away from me! Watch yourself — do not see my face again, because on the day you see my face you will die."
And Moses said, "You have spoken rightly. I will not see your face again."

chapters.title: About Midnight I Am Going Out
chapters.html:
Exodus 11

1And the LORD said to Moses, "One more blow I will bring on Pharaoh and on Egypt. After that he will send you away from here. When he sends you away, it will be complete — he will drive you out of here altogether.

2Speak now in the ears of the people, and let every man ask from his neighbor, and every woman from her neighbor, objects of silver and objects of gold."

3And the LORD gave the people favor in the eyes of Egypt. Also the man Moses was very great in the land of Egypt, in the eyes of Pharaoh's servants and in the eyes of the people.

4And Moses said, "This is what the LORD says: About midnight I am going out into the middle of Egypt.

5And every firstborn in the land of Egypt will die — from the firstborn of Pharaoh sitting on his throne to the firstborn of the slave girl who is behind the millstones, and every firstborn of the animals.

6And there will be a great cry in all the land of Egypt, such as there has never been and such as there will never be again.

7But against all the sons of Israel not a dog will sharpen its tongue — not against man or beast — so that you may know that the LORD makes a distinction between Egypt and Israel.

8And all these servants of yours will come down to me and bow to me, saying, 'Get out, you and all the people who follow you!' And after that I will go out." And he went out from Pharaoh in burning anger.

9And the LORD said to Moses, "Pharaoh will not listen to you — so that My wonders may be many in the land of Egypt."

10And Moses and Aaron did all these wonders before Pharaoh, and the LORD made Pharaoh's heart strong, and he did not send the sons of Israel out of his land.

Notes

  • v1 "one more blow" — nega, and the ordinary meaning of the word is a touch. It is used for a skin affliction and for a stroke of judgment, but the root is contact. After hail and locusts and darkness, the last one is named as a touch.

  • v1 "he will drive you out of here altogether" — garesh yegaresh, the verb doubled for force, and it is the third time in three chapters. God promised it in 6:1 — with a strong hand he will drive them out. Pharaoh did it to Moses and Aaron personally in 10:11. Here it is promised for the whole people. The king's own characteristic act becomes the mechanism of his defeat.

  • v2 "let every man ask from his neighbor" — re'ehu, his neighbor, and the verb is sha'al, to ask. Older English Bibles print borrow, which turns the scene into a deception. The Hebrew does not say borrow. It says ask, and the next verse says they were given the things because Egypt looked on them with favor. At 3:22 only the women were told to ask; now it is everyone.

  • v3 "the man Moses was very great in the land of Egypt" — the narrator steps outside the story for one clause to say how Moses was regarded. It is the only such assessment in the book, and it is startling: the wanted fugitive of chapter 2 is now a figure of standing in Pharaoh's own court, among the servants who had already turned on their king in 10:7.

  • v4 "About midnight I am going out into the middle of Egypt" — no staff, no Aaron, no outstretched hand. Every other plague came through an instrument. This one God performs in person, and the verb He uses for it is yatsa, to go out — the same verb used throughout the book for Israel going out of Egypt. God goes out into Egypt so that Israel can go out of it.

  • v5 "from the firstborn of Pharaoh... to the firstborn of the slave girl behind the millstones" — the top and the bottom of Egyptian society, named by where they sit: one on a throne, one behind a handmill. The slave girl is as Egyptian as the king, and the text makes a point of including her loss.

  • v6 "a great cry" — tse'aqah gedolah. It is Israel's word. The sons of Israel groaned from the labor and cried out, and their cry went up to God (2:23); God said I have heard their cry (3:7). Egypt now makes the same sound. The book does not comment; it just uses the word again.

  • v7 "not a dog will sharpen its tongue" — lo yecheratz kelev leshono, and the idiom has no clean English. Charatz means to cut, sharpen, decide. Something between a dog whetting its tongue and a dog so much as growling. Whatever the precise picture, the claim is total silence on Israel's side of the night while Egypt is screaming.

  • v8 "and bow to me" — Moses says Pharaoh's officials will bow to him, not to God. It is the most personal thing he has said in the whole contest, and it comes immediately before the only sentence in the book that reports his temper.

  • v8 "in burning anger" — ba-chori af, literally in the burning of the nose, which is how Hebrew says rage. This is the first time Moses is angry. It is also the last conversation: he told Pharaoh in 10:29 that he would not see his face again, and he does not.

  • v9 "so that My wonders may be many" — the stated reason for the whole sequence, placed at the end of it rather than the beginning. The plagues were not ten attempts that failed nine times. By this account the number was the point.

chapters.title: This Month Is the Head of Months
chapters.html:
Exodus 12

1And the LORD said to Moses and to Aaron in the land of Egypt:

2"This month is for you the head of months. It is the first for you, of the months of the year.

3Speak to the whole assembly of Israel: On the tenth of this month, let them take for themselves, each man, a lamb for a father's house — a lamb for a household.

4And if the household is too small for a lamb, then he and his neighbor nearest his house shall take one, by the number of people. You shall count for the lamb according to what each one eats.

5A lamb without blemish, male, a year old, shall be yours. You may take it from the sheep or from the goats.

6And you shall keep it until the fourteenth day of this month, and the whole congregation of the assembly of Israel shall slaughter it between the evenings.

7And they shall take some of the blood and put it on the two doorposts and on the lintel, on the houses where they eat it.

8And they shall eat the meat that night, roasted with fire, with unleavened bread, with bitter herbs they shall eat it.

9Do not eat any of it raw, or boiled at all in water, but roasted with fire — its head with its legs and with its inner parts.

10And you shall not leave any of it until morning. And whatever is left of it until morning you shall burn with fire.

11And this is how you shall eat it: your waists belted, your sandals on your feet, and your staff in your hand. And you shall eat it in haste. It is a Passover to the LORD.

12And I will pass through the land of Egypt that night, and I will strike down every firstborn in the land of Egypt, from man to beast. And against all the gods of Egypt I will carry out judgments. I am the LORD.

13And the blood will be a sign for you on the houses where you are. And I will see the blood, and I will pass over you, and there will be no blow of destruction against you when I strike the land of Egypt.

A Memorial

14And this day will be a memorial for you, and you shall keep it as a feast to the LORD. Through your generations, as a lasting statute, you shall keep it.

15Seven days you shall eat unleavened bread. On the very first day you shall put away leaven from your houses, because anyone who eats what is leavened, from the first day to the seventh day — that person will be cut off from Israel.

16And on the first day there will be a holy assembly, and on the seventh day a holy assembly for you. No work shall be done on them, except what every person must eat — only that may be prepared for you.

17And you shall keep the Unleavened Bread, because on this very day I brought your divisions out of the land of Egypt. And you shall keep this day through your generations, as a lasting statute.

18In the first month, on the fourteenth day of the month in the evening, you shall eat unleavened bread, until the twenty-first day of the month in the evening.

19For seven days no leaven shall be found in your houses, because anyone who eats what is leavened — that person will be cut off from the assembly of Israel, whether a foreigner or a native of the land.

20You shall eat nothing leavened. In all your dwellings you shall eat unleavened bread."

Draw Out and Take

21And Moses called for all the elders of Israel and said to them, "Draw out and take for yourselves flocks for your families, and slaughter the Passover.

22And you shall take a bunch of hyssop and dip it in the blood that is in the basin, and touch the lintel and the two doorposts with the blood that is in the basin. And none of you shall go out from the doorway of his house until morning.

23And the LORD will pass through to strike Egypt, and He will see the blood on the lintel and on the two doorposts, and the LORD will pass over the doorway, and He will not let the destroyer come into your houses to strike.

24And you shall keep this thing as a decree for you and for your sons forever.

25And it will be, when you come to the land that the LORD will give you as He promised, that you shall keep this service.

26And it will be, when your sons say to you, 'What does this service mean to you?' —

27you shall say, 'It is the sacrifice of the Passover to the LORD, who passed over the houses of the sons of Israel in Egypt when He struck Egypt, and He rescued our houses.'" And the people bowed down and worshiped.

28And the sons of Israel went and did as the LORD had commanded Moses and Aaron — so they did.

At Midnight

29And it came to pass at midnight that the LORD struck down every firstborn in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of Pharaoh sitting on his throne to the firstborn of the captive who was in the dungeon, and every firstborn of the animals.

30And Pharaoh got up in the night, he and all his servants and all Egypt, and there was a great cry in Egypt, because there was no house where there was not someone dead.

31And he called for Moses and Aaron at night and said, "Get up, get out from among my people, both you and the sons of Israel! And go, serve the LORD as you said.

32Take your flocks and your herds too, as you said, and go. And bless me also."

33And Egypt pressed hard on the people to hurry them out of the land, because they said, "We are all dead men."

34And the people carried their dough before it was leavened, their kneading bowls bound up in their cloaks on their shoulders.

35And the sons of Israel did as Moses said, and they asked from Egypt objects of silver and objects of gold and clothing.

36And the LORD gave the people favor in the eyes of Egypt, and they let them have what they asked. And they stripped Egypt bare.

37And the sons of Israel set out from Rameses toward Succoth, about six hundred thousand men on foot, besides children.

38And a great mixed crowd also went up with them, and flocks and herds, a very great amount of livestock.

39And they baked the dough they had brought out of Egypt into flat cakes of unleavened bread, because it had not risen — because they were driven out of Egypt and could not wait, and they had not even made provisions for themselves.

40And the time the sons of Israel lived in Egypt was four hundred and thirty years.

41And it came to pass at the end of four hundred and thirty years — on this very day all the divisions of the LORD went out from the land of Egypt.

42It is a night of watching for the LORD, to bring them out of the land of Egypt. This is that night for the LORD, a watching for all the sons of Israel through their generations.

One Law

43And the LORD said to Moses and Aaron, "This is the statute of the Passover. No foreigner shall eat of it.

44But every man's slave, bought with money — when you have circumcised him, then he may eat of it.

45A resident and a hired man shall not eat of it.

46It shall be eaten in one house. You shall not take any of the meat outside the house, and you shall not break a bone of it.

47The whole assembly of Israel shall keep it.

48And when a foreigner lives with you and would keep the Passover to the LORD, let every male belonging to him be circumcised, and then he may come near to keep it, and he will be like a native of the land. But no uncircumcised person shall eat of it.

49There shall be one law for the native and for the foreigner living among you."

50And all the sons of Israel did as the LORD had commanded Moses and Aaron — so they did.

51And it came to pass on this very day that the LORD brought the sons of Israel out of the land of Egypt by their divisions.

Notes

  • v2 "This month is for you the head of months" — before any instruction about the meal, the calendar is reset. The first thing given to a people who are still slaves is not freedom but a new way of counting time, and the count starts from the month they leave. Everything in their year will now be measured from this.

  • v5 "from the sheep or from the goats" — the Hebrew word seh covers both, and the verse says so outright. Centuries of art and translation have made this a lamb; the text permits a kid, and Genesis 22 and the goat of the Day of Atonement both stand behind the choice.

  • v6 "between the evenings" — bein ha-arbayim, two evenings, and nobody has ever been certain which two. It has been read as the time between sunset and full dark, and as the time between the sun's decline and sunset. The dispute is old and the Hebrew does not decide it.

  • v8 "with bitter herbs" — merorim, from marar, to be bitter. It is the root of the sentence in 1:14: and they made their lives bitter with hard slavery. The taste on the table that night is the name of what they are leaving.

  • v9 "or boiled at all in water" — the word is bashal, to boil, and the prohibition is emphatic. Deuteronomy 16:7, giving the same festival, says u-vishalta ve-akhalta — you shall boil it and eat it, the same verb, as a command. Both sentences are in the Bible. Later tradition reconciled them by widening bashal to mean cooking of any kind; the plainest reading of the two verses is that they disagree.

  • v11 "your waists belted, your sandals on your feet, your staff in your hand" — the meal is eaten dressed to leave. It is the only sacrifice in the Bible with a dress code, and the code is traveling clothes.

  • v12 "against all the gods of Egypt I will carry out judgments" — the only verse in the sequence that names what the plagues are against. Not a king and not a nation: the gods.

  • v13 "I will pass over you" — u-fasachti, and this is the verb the festival is named for. Its meaning is genuinely unsettled. It can be read as pass over, or skip, or limp; but Isaiah 31:5 puts it in a chain with three protective verbs — shielding and rescuing, pasoach and delivering — which suggests something closer to standing over to protect than to walking past. English chose pass over long ago, and the name of the feast in every European language follows it.

  • v13 "no blow of destruction" — and in v23 the destroyer, ha-mashchit. The text speaks of the destroyer as something the LORD does not let into the houses. Who or what it is, the book does not say.

  • v22 "the blood that is in the basin" — ba-saf, and saf means both a basin and a threshold. So the blood is in a bowl, or it is on the doorstep. Both readings are ancient, and either makes sense of the scene: the doorway is marked on three sides, and possibly on four.

  • v22 "none of you shall go out from the doorway of his house until morning" — the one thing Israel must actively do that night is stay inside. The deliverance is not something they take part in. It happens over their heads while they eat standing up.

  • v26 "when your sons say to you, 'What does this service mean to you?'" — the second instruction in three chapters to prepare an answer for a child (see 10:2). The ritual is designed from the outset around a question it expects to be asked, and the seder's four questions grow directly out of this verse and its parallels in 13:8 and 13:14.

  • v29 "the firstborn of the captive who was in the dungeon" — in 11:5 the bottom of the scale was the slave girl behind the millstones. Here it is a prisoner in a pit. The announcement and the event name different people at the low end, and the effect is the same: the reach goes all the way down.

  • v30 "there was no house where there was not someone dead" — the double negative is in the Hebrew, and it lands harder than a plain statement would. And tse'aqah gedolah, a great cry, is the phrase used of Israel's suffering in 2:23 and 3:7.

  • v32 "And bless me also" — the last words Pharaoh speaks in the book. The man who asked Who is the LORD? I do not know the LORD (5:2) ends by asking the LORD's prophet for a blessing, in the middle of the night, with his son dead.

  • v33 "Egypt pressed hard on the people" — va-techezaq mitsrayim, from chazaq, to be strong. It is the hardening verb, and here it is Egypt being strong — not to hold Israel, but to push them out the door. The word that kept them in is the word that expels them.

  • v34 "their kneading bowls bound up in their cloaks" — mish'arotam, and the last time that word appeared, the frogs were in them (8:3). What Egypt's plague filled, Israel now carries out on its shoulders.

  • v36 "they stripped Egypt bare" — va-yenatslu, from natsal, the verb for rescue. God came down to rescue Israel from Egypt's hand (3:8); Israel now rescues Egypt of its silver. The book has been setting this word against itself since the bush, and this is where the two senses meet.

  • v38 "a great mixed crowd" — erev rav, from a root meaning to mix. Whoever they were, the people who leave Egypt are not all Israelites, and the text says so in the same breath as the census number. The law four verses later, one law for the native and for the foreigner, is written for people who are already walking with them.

  • v39 "because they were driven out" — gorshu, and that is the fourth appearance of garash since 6:1. Unleavened bread is explained here not as a symbol but as a consequence: nobody had time to let dough rise.

  • v41 "on this very day" — be-etsem ha-yom ha-zeh, and the same phrase closes the chapter at v51. Etsem is the word for a bone, and by extension the substance or very thing itself. The idiom means on that exact day, and the chapter uses it three times, fixing the date the way the first verse fixed the month.

  • v46 "you shall not break a bone of it" — ve-etsem lo tishberu vo. John 19:36 quotes this line of the Passover law about the body of Jesus on the cross: a bone of him shall not be broken.

  • v49 "one law for the native and for the foreigner" — torah achat. Immediately after a rule excluding the uncircumcised, the text states the principle that the rule is not about ancestry. The door is circumcision, not birth, and once through it a foreigner is like a native of the land.

chapters.title: The Opener of Every Womb
chapters.html:
Exodus 13

1And the LORD spoke to Moses:

2"Set apart to Me every firstborn, the opener of every womb among the sons of Israel, in man and in beast. It is Mine."

3And Moses said to the people, "Remember this day, on which you came out of Egypt, out of the house of slaves, because with a strong hand the LORD brought you out of here. And nothing leavened shall be eaten.

4Today you are going out, in the month of Aviv.

5And it will be, when the LORD brings you to the land of the Canaanite and the Hittite and the Amorite and the Hivite and the Jebusite, which He swore to your fathers to give you — a land flowing with milk and honey — that you shall keep this service in this month.

6Seven days you shall eat unleavened bread, and on the seventh day there will be a feast to the LORD.

7Unleavened bread shall be eaten through the seven days, and nothing leavened shall be seen with you, and no leaven shall be seen with you in all your territory.

8And you shall tell your son on that day, 'It is because of what the LORD did for me when I came out of Egypt.'

9And it will be a sign for you on your hand, and a reminder between your eyes, so that the instruction of the LORD may be in your mouth — because with a strong hand the LORD brought you out of Egypt.

10And you shall keep this statute at its appointed time, from year to year.

Every Firstborn Is Mine

11"And it will be, when the LORD brings you to the land of the Canaanite, as He swore to you and to your fathers, and gives it to you,

12that you shall set apart to the LORD every opener of the womb. And every firstling dropped by an animal that belongs to you — the males are the LORD's.

13And every firstling of a donkey you shall redeem with a lamb, and if you do not redeem it, you shall break its neck. And every firstborn of man among your sons you shall redeem.

14And it will be, when your son asks you tomorrow, 'What is this?' — you shall say to him, 'With a strong hand the LORD brought us out of Egypt, out of the house of slaves.

15And it came to pass, when Pharaoh made it hard to send us away, that the LORD killed every firstborn in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of man to the firstborn of beast. That is why I sacrifice to the LORD every male that opens the womb, and every firstborn of my sons I redeem.'

16And it will be a sign on your hand and a band between your eyes, because with a strong hand the LORD brought us out of Egypt."

The Long Way Round

17And it came to pass, when Pharaoh sent the people away, that God did not lead them by the way of the land of the Philistines, though it was near — because God said, "The people may change their minds when they see war, and go back to Egypt."

18And God took the people around by the way of the wilderness, to the Sea of Reeds. And the sons of Israel went up out of the land of Egypt in ranks.

19And Moses took the bones of Joseph with him, because he had made the sons of Israel swear, saying, "God will surely attend to you, and you shall bring my bones up from here with you."

20And they set out from Succoth and camped at Etham, at the edge of the wilderness.

21And the LORD went before them by day in a pillar of cloud to lead them on the way, and by night in a pillar of fire to give them light — so they could travel by day and by night.

22The pillar of cloud did not move away by day, nor the pillar of fire by night, from before the people.

Notes

  • v2 "the opener of every womb" — peter kol rechem, and the Hebrew is anatomical rather than ceremonial. Not the eldest son but the one that opened the body. That is why the rule covers animals in the same breath, and why v12 repeats it for a firstling dropped by a beast.

  • v4 "the month of Aviv" — aviv means the barley in the ear, green and not yet hard. Four chapters back, the hail struck the flax and the barley because the barley was aviv (9:31). The month of the exodus is named for the crop stage that dated the seventh plague, and the same word does both jobs.

  • v3, 14 "the house of slaves" — beit avadim. Not a condition but an address: the house you lived in. And avadim is the same word as the service Israel is now to render the LORD in v5 — avodah. They leave one master's house to serve another, and Hebrew uses one root for both.

  • v8 "what the LORD did for me" — not for them, not for us: for me. A man who was not there says the exodus happened to him personally. This single word is the hinge of the whole Passover liturgy, which requires each person in every generation to say it in the first person.

  • v9 "a sign on your hand, and a reminder between your eyes" — the sentence later Judaism takes literally, as the leather boxes worn on the arm and forehead. Whether the verse was meant as a figure of speech or an instruction is not decidable from the words; both readings are old.

  • v16 "a band between your eyes" — totafot, and the word occurs three times in the entire Hebrew Bible: here, Deuteronomy 6:8, and Deuteronomy 11:18 — all three in this same formula and nowhere else. Its meaning is unrecovered. Bands, frontlets, ornaments have all been proposed. Nothing in Hebrew settles it, because the word has no other occurrence to be compared with.

  • v13 "you shall break its neck" — the donkey cannot be sacrificed, because it is not a clean animal; but it is a firstling and so belongs to God. The law gives two ways to hand it over: buy it back with a lamb, or destroy it. There is no option to keep it.

  • v17 "God did not lead them... the people may change their minds" — two different roots that come out on the page as the same three letters, נחם. Nacham here is lead them; yinnachem in the second half is change their mind, relent. A reader of the consonants sees the same word twice in one verse, doing opposite work.

  • v17 "though it was near" — the coastal road to Canaan was a week's walk. The text says plainly that God chose the long way on purpose, and gives the reason: a people fresh out of slavery will turn around the first time they are shot at.

  • v18 "in ranks" — chamushim, and the word is genuinely uncertain. It is spelled with the same consonants as chamishim, fifty — the word used for the officers over fifties in 18:21 and for the fifty loops of the tabernacle curtain in 26:5. So the phrase has been read as in battle order, in fives, and armed. The letters do not choose.

  • v19 "the bones of Joseph" — Genesis ends with Joseph making this exact demand: God will surely attend to you, and you shall bring my bones up from here (50:25). The phrase he used, paqod yifqod, is the one God turned into the past tense at the bush — I have surely attended. Four hundred years later Moses walks out of Egypt carrying a coffin, and the book records it in one verse between two travel notes.

  • v21 "a pillar of cloud... a pillar of fire" — the text does not describe two things. It is one presence, seen as cloud in daylight and as fire in the dark, and v22 says neither ever left. What it does is not protect or fight. It makes travel possible at any hour.

speech.text: Exodus 13
And the LORD spoke to Moses:
"Set apart to Me every firstborn, the opener of every womb among the sons of Israel, in man and in beast. It is Mine."

And Moses said to the people, "Remember this day, on which you came out of Egypt, out of the house of slaves, because with a strong hand the LORD brought you out of here. And nothing leavened shall be eaten.
Today you are going out, in the month of Aviv.

And it will be, when the LORD brings you to the land of the Canaanite and the Hittite and the Amorite and the Hivite and the Jebusite, which He swore to your fathers to give you — a land flowing with milk and honey — that you shall keep this service in this month.
Seven days you shall eat unleavened bread, and on the seventh day there will be a feast to the LORD.
Unleavened bread shall be eaten through the seven days, and nothing leavened shall be seen with you, and no leaven shall be seen with you in all your territory.
And you shall tell your son on that day, 'It is because of what the LORD did for me when I came out of Egypt.'
And it will be a sign for you on your hand, and a reminder between your eyes, so that the instruction of the LORD may be in your mouth — because with a strong hand the LORD brought you out of Egypt.
And you shall keep this statute at its appointed time, from year to year.
Every Firstborn Is Mine
"And it will be, when the LORD brings you to the land of the Canaanite, as He swore to you and to your fathers, and gives it to you,
that you shall set apart to the LORD every opener of the womb. And every firstling dropped by an animal that belongs to you — the males are the LORD's.
And every firstling of a donkey you shall redeem with a lamb, and if you do not redeem it, you shall break its neck. And every firstborn of man among your sons you shall redeem.
And it will be, when your son asks you tomorrow, 'What is this?' — you shall say to him, 'With a strong hand the LORD brought us out of Egypt, out of the house of slaves.

And it came to pass, when Pharaoh made it hard to send us away, that the LORD killed every firstborn in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of man to the firstborn of beast. That is why I sacrifice to the LORD every male that opens the womb, and every firstborn of my sons I redeem.'
And it will be a sign on your hand and a band between your eyes, because with a strong hand the LORD brought us out of Egypt."
The Long Way Round

And it came to pass, when Pharaoh sent the people away, that God did not lead them by the way of the land of the Philistines, though it was near — because God said, "The people may change their minds when they see war, and go back to Egypt."
And God took the people around by the way of the wilderness, to the Sea of Reeds. And the sons of Israel went up out of the land of Egypt in ranks.
And Moses took the bones of Joseph with him, because he had made the sons of Israel swear, saying, "God will surely attend to you, and you shall bring my bones up from here with you."
And they set out from Succoth and camped at Etham, at the edge of the wilderness.
And the LORD went before them by day in a pillar of cloud to lead them on the way, and by night in a pillar of fire to give them light — so they could travel by day and by night.
The pillar of cloud did not move away by day, nor the pillar of fire by night, from before the people.

chapters.title: The LORD Will Fight for You
chapters.html:
Exodus 14

1And the LORD spoke to Moses:

2"Speak to the sons of Israel, and let them turn back and camp before Pi-hahiroth, between Migdol and the sea, before Baal-zephon. Opposite it you shall camp, by the sea.

3And Pharaoh will say of the sons of Israel, 'They are wandering in confusion in the land. The wilderness has closed in on them.'

4And I will make Pharaoh's heart strong, and he will chase after them, and I will get My weight on Pharaoh and on all his army, and Egypt will know that I am the LORD." And they did so.

5And the king of Egypt was told that the people had fled, and the heart of Pharaoh and his servants turned against the people, and they said, "What is this we have done, sending Israel away from serving us?"

6And he harnessed his chariot and took his people with him.

7And he took six hundred chosen chariots, and all the chariots of Egypt, and officers over all of them.

8And the LORD made the heart of Pharaoh king of Egypt strong, and he chased after the sons of Israel — and the sons of Israel were going out with a high hand.

9And Egypt chased after them and overtook them camped by the sea — all Pharaoh's horses and chariots and his horsemen and his army — at Pi-hahiroth, before Baal-zephon.

Stand Still and See

10And Pharaoh drew near, and the sons of Israel lifted their eyes, and here — Egypt marching after them. And they were very afraid, and the sons of Israel cried out to the LORD.

11And they said to Moses, "Was it for lack of graves in Egypt that you took us away to die in the wilderness? What is this you have done to us, bringing us out of Egypt?

12Is this not the thing we said to you in Egypt: 'Leave us alone and let us serve Egypt'? For it would be better for us to serve Egypt than to die in the wilderness."

13And Moses said to the people, "Do not be afraid. Stand still and see the deliverance of the LORD, which He will work for you today — for the Egyptians you see today, you will never see them again.

14The LORD will fight for you, and you — be silent."

15And the LORD said to Moses, "What are you crying out to Me for? Speak to the sons of Israel, and let them move on.

16And you — lift up your staff and stretch out your hand over the sea and split it, and the sons of Israel will come into the middle of the sea on dry ground.

17And I — here, I am making the heart of Egypt strong, and they will come in after them. And I will get My weight on Pharaoh and on all his army, on his chariots and on his horsemen.

18And Egypt will know that I am the LORD, when I get My weight on Pharaoh, on his chariots and on his horsemen."

The Sea

19And the messenger of God who was going before the camp of Israel moved and went behind them, and the pillar of cloud moved from before them and stood behind them.

20And it came between the camp of Egypt and the camp of Israel. And there was the cloud and the darkness, and it lit up the night, and neither came near the other all night.

21And Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and the LORD drove the sea back with a strong east wind all night, and made the sea into dry ground, and the waters were split.

22And the sons of Israel came into the middle of the sea on dry ground, and the waters were a wall for them on their right and on their left.

23And Egypt chased and came in after them — all Pharaoh's horses, his chariots and his horsemen — into the middle of the sea.

24And it came to pass in the morning watch that the LORD looked down on the camp of Egypt through the pillar of fire and cloud, and threw the camp of Egypt into confusion.

25And He took off the wheels of their chariots, and drove them heavily. And Egypt said, "Let me flee from before Israel, because the LORD is fighting for them against Egypt."

26And the LORD said to Moses, "Stretch out your hand over the sea, and let the waters come back over Egypt, over its chariots and over its horsemen."

27And Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and toward morning the sea came back to its steady flow. And Egypt was fleeing to meet it, and the LORD shook Egypt off into the middle of the sea.

28And the waters came back and covered the chariots and the horsemen, all of Pharaoh's army that had come after them into the sea. Not one of them was left.

29And the sons of Israel walked on dry ground in the middle of the sea, and the waters were a wall for them on their right and on their left.

30And the LORD saved Israel that day from the hand of Egypt, and Israel saw Egypt dead on the shore of the sea.

31And Israel saw the great hand that the LORD had worked against Egypt, and the people feared the LORD, and they believed in the LORD and in Moses His servant.

Notes

  • v4 "I will get My weight on Pharaoh" — ikkavdah, and this is the root the book has been building all along: kaved, heavy. It is the word for Pharaoh's heavy heart (7:14), for Moses' heavy mouth (4:10), for the heavy hail and the heavy plague (9:18, 9:3). Here the same root means glory — because in Hebrew, glory is weight, what has substance and cannot be brushed aside. The word that described Pharaoh's stubbornness now describes God's honor, taken on him. English needs two unrelated words; Hebrew uses one and the whole book turns on it.

  • v5 "the heart of Pharaoh and his servants turned" — va-yehafekh, to overturn. Not hardened this time. Flipped. And the reason given is economic in the plainest terms: we have lost our workforce.

  • v8 "with a high hand" — be-yad ramah. The phrase means openly, defiantly, in full view — not sneaking out. Egypt thinks they fled (v5); the narrator says they marched.

  • v11 "Was it for lack of graves in Egypt?" — the first complaint in the wilderness, and it is sarcasm. Egypt is the land of tombs; it is what Egypt is famous for. They are telling Moses there was no shortage of places to be buried back there.

  • v12 "it would be better for us to serve Egypt" — la'avod, the same verb as serving the LORD. The argument of the whole book, stated by the people in one sentence: they are not choosing between slavery and freedom, but between masters, and they would rather have the one that fed them.

  • v14 "and you — be silent" — tacharishun, from charash, to be silent, also to be deaf. It is the only instruction Israel is given at the sea, and it is to do nothing and say nothing.

  • v16 "and split it" — u-veqa'ehu, from baqa. It is the flood's verb: in Genesis 7:11 all the fountains of the great deep were split open, and the water came up to drown the world. Here the same verb opens water to save a people. The one time the Bible uses baqa of a sea before this, everyone died.

  • v20 "the cloud and the darkness, and it lit up the night" — the Hebrew is compressed and hard: one clause has cloud and darkness, the next has light. The oldest translations already differ on who gets which. The plainest reading is that the same pillar was darkness on Egypt's side and light on Israel's.

  • v21 "a strong east wind all night" — ruach qadim, and it is the wind from 10:13, which blew all that day and all that night to bring the locusts. Same wind, same duration, opposite service. Also worth hearing: ruach is breath, wind and spirit, and the sea is opened by the same word that hovers over the water in Genesis 1:2.

  • v22 "the waters were a wall" — chomah, a city wall. Not a bank or a heap: the word for fortification. Israel walks through a corridor with defensive walls on both sides, and the thing defending them is the sea.

  • v24 "the morning watch" — the last third of the night, before dawn. The whole crossing happens in the dark, and the destruction comes at the moment it becomes possible to see.

  • v25 "and drove them heavily" — bi-khvedut, from kaved again. The Egyptians are now the ones moving under weight. The root has run from Pharaoh's heart, to God's glory in v4, to the dragging of the chariots — three turns of one word inside twenty verses.

  • v30 "the LORD saved Israel" — va-yosha, from yasha, the root behind the names Joshua and Jesus. Moses first used it for seven Midianite women at a well (2:17). Here it is used of a nation, and v13 had already promised it as a noun: the deliverance of the LORD, yeshu'at YHWH.

  • v31 "they believed in the LORD and in Moses His servant" — the book's first statement that the people believe. It comes after the rescue, not before it, and it names Moses alongside God. In chapter 4 the question was whether they would believe him at all.

chapters.title: The Song at the Sea
chapters.html:
Exodus 15

1Then Moses and the sons of Israel sang this song to the LORD, and they said:

I will sing to the LORD, for He is high, high above —
horse and its rider He has thrown into the sea.

2My strength and my song is Yah,
and He has become my deliverance.
This is my God, and I will praise Him,
the God of my father, and I will lift Him high.

3The LORD is a man of war.
The LORD is His name.

4Pharaoh's chariots and his army He cast into the sea,
and the pick of his officers were drowned in the Sea of Reeds.

5The deeps covered them.
They went down into the depths like a stone.

6Your right hand, LORD, is majestic in power.
Your right hand, LORD, shatters the enemy.

7And in the greatness of Your rising You tear down those who stand against You.
You send out Your burning anger — it eats them like stubble.

8And by the breath of Your nostrils the waters were heaped up.
The flowing waters stood like a wall.
The deeps congealed in the heart of the sea.

9The enemy said, "I will chase, I will overtake, I will divide the spoil.
My appetite will be full of them.
I will draw my sword. My hand will drive them out."

10You blew with Your breath — the sea covered them.
They sank like lead in the mighty waters.

11Who is like You among the gods, LORD?
Who is like You — majestic in holiness,
fearful in praises, doing wonders?

12You stretched out Your right hand.
The earth swallowed them.

13In Your faithful love You led the people You redeemed.
In Your strength You guided them to Your holy dwelling.

14The peoples heard. They shook.
Writhing seized those who live in Philistia.

15Then the chiefs of Edom were terrified.
Trembling took hold of the rams of Moab.
All who live in Canaan melted away.

16Terror and dread fell on them.
By the greatness of Your arm they were still as a stone —
until Your people passed over, LORD,
until the people You made Your own passed over.

17You will bring them in and plant them on the mountain of Your inheritance —
the place You made for Your dwelling, LORD,
the sanctuary, Lord, that Your hands established.

18The LORD will reign forever and ever.

19For Pharaoh's horses went into the sea with his chariots and his horsemen, and the LORD brought the waters of the sea back over them. And the sons of Israel walked on dry ground in the middle of the sea.

20And Miriam the prophetess, Aaron's sister, took the tambourine in her hand, and all the women went out after her with tambourines and with dancing.

21And Miriam answered them:

Sing to the LORD, for He is high, high above —
horse and its rider He has thrown into the sea.

Bitter Water

22And Moses made Israel set out from the Sea of Reeds, and they went out into the wilderness of Shur, and they walked three days in the wilderness and found no water.

23And they came to Marah, and they could not drink water from Marah, because it was bitter. That is why its name was called Marah.

24And the people grumbled against Moses, saying, "What are we to drink?"

25And he cried out to the LORD, and the LORD showed him a tree, and he threw it into the water, and the water became sweet. There He made for them a statute and a rule, and there He tested them.

26And He said, "If you will listen hard to the voice of the LORD your God, and do what is right in His eyes, and give ear to His commands and keep all His statutes, then every sickness I put on Egypt I will not put on you — because I am the LORD your healer."

27And they came to Elim, and there were twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees, and they camped there by the water.

Notes

  • v1 "Then Moses... sang" — the Hebrew verb is yashir, which is the future form: then Moses will sing. Hebrew does use this form for past narration in poetry, and the sense here is past. But the oddity is real and old: readers as far back as the Talmud have taken it as a hint that the song is also still to be sung.

  • v1 "for He is high, high above" — ga'oh ga'ah, the verb doubled. Ga'ah is to rise up, to be lifted, and it is used of water swelling. The first line of the song describes God with the word for a rising tide.

  • v2 "Yah" — the short form of the divine name, and this is its first appearance in the Bible. Not YHWH but Yah, two letters, the form that survives in hallelu-Yah and at the end of names like Isaiah and Elijah. The oldest poem in the book uses the oldest form of the name.

  • v2 "my strength and my song" — ozzi ve-zimrat, and zimrat will not settle. It is the word for song or music, but there is a second root spelled the same that means strength or protection — which would make the line my strength and my might. Both readings are defensible and both are ancient.

  • v2 "I will praise Him" — ve-anvehu, from a root that gives both naveh, a dwelling or pasture, and a verb for beautifying. So the line has been read I will glorify Him and I will make Him a dwelling. Verse 13 then uses the noun outright — Your holy dwelling — which suggests the poet had the second sense in earshot.

  • v3 "The LORD is a man of war" — ish milchamah, blunt and unhedged. The Greek Septuagint could not leave it and rendered it the Lord, crushing wars. The Hebrew says man of war, and this rendering keeps it.

  • v5, v16 "like a stone" — the Egyptians go down like a stone in v5; the nations of Canaan are made still like a stone in v16. The song uses one image twice, for sinking and for freezing in place.

  • v8 "by the breath of Your nostrils" — ruach appekha. The prose account said an east wind blew all night (14:21). The poem says God exhaled. Same event, and ruach is the same word: wind, breath, spirit.

  • v8 "the deeps congealed" — tehomot, the same word as the deep over which the Spirit hovered in Genesis 1:2, and qafa, to thicken or curdle. The poem's picture is not of a corridor with two walls. It is of water turning solid.

  • v9 "I will chase, I will overtake, I will divide the spoil" — six short verbs in a row with nothing between them, and every one is first person. The enemy's whole speech is a man listing what he is about to take. The next verse is one breath from God, and it ends.

  • v11 "among the gods" — ba-elim. The song does not say the other gods do not exist; it asks who among them compares. That is what the Hebrew says, and it is older than the theology that later grew around it.

  • v12 "the earth swallowed them" — tivla'emo, from bala. Aaron's staff swallowed the magicians' staffs in 7:12 with this verb. The contest that began with a swallowing ends with one.

  • v13 "Your faithful love" — chesed, the hardest word in the Hebrew Bible to render: loyalty, kindness, covenant-faithfulness, the thing a party does because of a bond rather than because it must. No single English word holds it.

  • v17 "the mountain of Your inheritance... the sanctuary" — a temple, on a mountain, built by God's hands. There is no temple yet, no land, and no Jerusalem. The song is standing somewhere later than the story it tells.

  • v20 "Miriam the prophetess, Aaron's sister" — she is called Aaron's sister, not Moses'. She is also called a prophetess, the first woman given that title in the Bible, and she is unnamed back in chapter 2 when she watches the basket.

  • v21 "Sing to the LORD" — Miriam's version is the song's first line with one change: Moses' I will sing becomes her imperative, Sing! Some readers take her couplet as the original and the long song as the expansion. What can be said is that the book gives the same words twice and gives her the command form.

  • v23 "Marah, because it was bitter" — marah, from marar. It is the root of and they made their lives bitter in 1:14, and of the bitter herbs, merorim, on the Passover table in 12:8. Three days out of Egypt, the first thing they find is the taste they just left.

  • v25 "the LORD showed him a tree" — va-yorehu, from yarah, to point, to throw, to instruct — and it is the root of torah. God instructs him with a tree, and in the same verse gives a statute and a rule. The pun is not decorative: the first teaching in the wilderness is about water.

  • v26 "I am the LORD your healer" — rof'ekha, from rafa, the root in the name Raphael. The promise is framed as an exemption: the diseases of Egypt will not follow them. The sentence assumes the plagues were aimed, not general.

  • v27 "twelve springs and seventy palm trees" — twelve for the tribes and seventy for the elders of Israel and the nations of Genesis 10 is how later readers heard it; the text just gives the count. What the verse does is put a place of abundant water immediately after a place of bitter water, and say they camped there.

And Miriam answered them:
Bitter Water
And Moses made Israel set out from the Sea of Reeds, and they went out into the wilderness of Shur, and they walked three days in the wilderness and found no water.
And they came to Marah, and they could not drink water from Marah, because it was bitter. That is why its name was called Marah.
And the people grumbled against Moses, saying, "What are we to drink?"
And he cried out to the LORD, and the LORD showed him a tree, and he threw it into the water, and the water became sweet. There He made for them a statute and a rule, and there He tested them.

And He said, "If you will listen hard to the voice of the LORD your God, and do what is right in His eyes, and give ear to His commands and keep all His statutes, then every sickness I put on Egypt I will not put on you — because I am the LORD your healer."
And they came to Elim, and there were twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees, and they camped there by the water.

chapters.title: What Is It?
chapters.html:
Exodus 16

1And they set out from Elim, and the whole assembly of the sons of Israel came to the wilderness of Sin, which is between Elim and Sinai, on the fifteenth day of the second month after they came out of the land of Egypt.

2And the whole assembly of the sons of Israel grumbled against Moses and against Aaron in the wilderness.

3And the sons of Israel said to them, "If only we had died by the hand of the LORD in the land of Egypt, when we sat by the pot of meat, when we ate bread until we were full — because you have brought us out into this wilderness to kill this whole assembly with hunger."

4And the LORD said to Moses, "Here — I am raining down bread from the sky for you. And the people shall go out and gather a day's portion in its day, so that I may test them, whether they will walk in My instruction or not.

5And it will be on the sixth day that they shall prepare what they bring in, and it will be double what they gather day by day."

6And Moses and Aaron said to all the sons of Israel, "Evening — and you will know that it was the LORD who brought you out of the land of Egypt.

7And morning — and you will see the weight of the LORD's glory, in His hearing your grumblings against the LORD. And what are we, that you grumble against us?"

8And Moses said, "When the LORD gives you meat to eat in the evening, and bread in the morning to be full — in the LORD's hearing your grumblings, which you are grumbling against Him — and what are we? Your grumblings are not against us but against the LORD."

9And Moses said to Aaron, "Say to the whole assembly of the sons of Israel, 'Come near before the LORD, because He has heard your grumblings.'"

10And it came to pass, as Aaron was speaking to the whole assembly of the sons of Israel, that they turned toward the wilderness — and here, the glory of the LORD appeared in the cloud.

11And the LORD spoke to Moses:

12"I have heard the grumblings of the sons of Israel. Speak to them: 'At twilight you will eat meat, and in the morning you will be full of bread, and you will know that I am the LORD your God.'"

What Is It?

13And it came to pass in the evening that quail came up and covered the camp, and in the morning there was a layer of dew around the camp.

14And the layer of dew went up, and here — on the face of the wilderness a fine, flaking thing, fine as frost on the ground.

15And the sons of Israel saw it and said to one another, "What is it?" — because they did not know what it was. And Moses said to them, "It is the bread that the LORD has given you to eat.

16This is the thing the LORD has commanded: gather of it, each according to what he eats, an omer a head, according to the number of your people. Each of you shall take for those in his tent."

17And the sons of Israel did so, and they gathered — some more, some less.

18And they measured it by the omer, and the one who gathered much had nothing over, and the one who gathered little had no lack. Each had gathered according to what he ate.

19And Moses said to them, "Let no one leave any of it until morning."

20But they did not listen to Moses, and some men left part of it until morning — and it bred worms and stank. And Moses was angry with them.

21And they gathered it morning by morning, each according to what he ate. And when the sun grew hot, it melted.

The Seventh Day

22And it came to pass on the sixth day that they gathered double bread, two omers for each person. And all the chiefs of the assembly came and told Moses.

23And he said to them, "This is what the LORD spoke: tomorrow is a rest, a holy sabbath to the LORD. Bake what you will bake and boil what you will boil, and all that is left over set aside for yourselves, to keep until morning."

24And they set it aside until morning, as Moses had commanded, and it did not stink, and there was no worm in it.

25And Moses said, "Eat it today, because today is a sabbath to the LORD. Today you will not find it in the field.

26Six days you shall gather it, and on the seventh day, the sabbath, there will be none."

27And it came to pass on the seventh day that some of the people went out to gather, and they found none.

28And the LORD said to Moses, "How long will you refuse to keep My commands and My instructions?

29See that the LORD has given you the sabbath — that is why He gives you bread for two days on the sixth day. Each of you stay where you are. Let no one go out from his place on the seventh day."

30And the people rested on the seventh day.

31And the house of Israel called its name Man. And it was like coriander seed, white, and its taste was like a wafer with honey.

32And Moses said, "This is the thing the LORD has commanded: a full omer of it is to be kept through your generations, so that they may see the bread I fed you in the wilderness when I brought you out of the land of Egypt."

33And Moses said to Aaron, "Take one jar and put a full omer of manna in it, and set it down before the LORD, to be kept through your generations."

34As the LORD commanded Moses, Aaron set it down before the Testimony, to be kept.

35And the sons of Israel ate the manna forty years, until they came to an inhabited land. They ate the manna until they came to the edge of the land of Canaan.

36And the omer is a tenth of an ephah.

Notes

  • v2 "grumbled" — the Hebrew here carries a ketiv/qere: the consonants as written are one form of the verb, and the reading tradition supplies another. The scribes kept both rather than choose. It is the first of many complaints in the wilderness, and the text cannot settle how to spell it.

  • v3 "when we sat by the pot of meat" — one pot, and slaves remembering it as plenty. The complaint is not that Egypt was good; it is that hunger is worse than slavery. Two chapters ago they preferred serving Egypt to dying at the sea (14:12). The argument has not changed, only the threat.

  • v4 "so that I may test them, whether they will walk in My instruction" — torah, before there is any law. The first test is not obedience to a command but whether people can take one day's food and not hoard.

  • v7 "the weight of the LORD's glory" — kevod, from kaved, heavy. It is the root of Pharaoh's heavy heart and of God's getting weight on Pharaoh at the sea (14:4). Here it is what the people will see in a cloud. The same three letters have now carried stubbornness, honor, and visible presence.

  • v14 "a fine, flaking thing" — daq mechuspas, and mechuspas occurs nowhere else in the Hebrew Bible. Nothing can be compared with it. Flaky, scaly, granular, peeled have all been proposed from the shape of the root and from the ancient translations. The word describing what the food looked like is a word nobody can define.

  • v15 "What is it?" — man hu. That is the question, and in v31 it becomes the name: they called its name Man. The thing they ate for forty years is called What-Is-It. English keeps the name as manna and loses the joke, which is that a nation was fed on a question.

  • v18 "the one who gathered much had nothing over, and the one who gathered little had no lack" — 2 Corinthians 8:15 quotes this verse exactly, in an appeal for a collection: as it is written, the one who had much did not have too much, and the one who had little did not have too little. Paul is using the manna as an argument about money.

  • v20 "it bred worms and stank" — va-yiv'ash, the stink verb again. The Nile stank with dead fish (7:21), the land stank with dead frogs (8:14), and Israel's foremen accused Moses of making them stink (5:21). Hoarded bread joins the list.

  • v21 "when the sun grew hot, it melted" — the food has a deadline at both ends. It cannot be gathered late, and it cannot be kept. Everything about it is designed to prevent storage.

  • v23 "a rest, a holy sabbath to the LORD" — the sabbath is commanded here, before Sinai, and it is not introduced as new. Moses says this is what the LORD spoke, as though the people should already know. The commandment at 20:8 will say remember.

  • v29 "let no one go out from his place" — the rule is given without explanation and became the basis for a whole body of later law about how far one may walk on the sabbath. The verse itself just says stay put.

  • v31 "like coriander seed, white, and its taste was like a wafer with honey" — the only description of it. Numbers 11:8 will say it tasted of oil-cake instead. The book that records both does not reconcile them.

  • v33 "one jar" — tsintsenet, another word that occurs nowhere else. A jar of an unknown kind, holding an unmeasurable food, kept in front of a Testimony that has not yet been given.

  • v34 "before the Testimony" — the ark does not exist yet; it is built in chapter 37. The verse is written by someone standing later, placing the jar where it will eventually go.

  • v36 "the omer is a tenth of an ephah" — an editor's footnote inside the verse. By the time this sentence was added, readers no longer knew how much an omer was, and someone converted it into a measure they did know.
