chapters.title: Is the LORD Among Us or Not?
chapters.html:
Exodus 17

Massah and Meribah

1And the whole assembly of the sons of Israel set out from the wilderness of Sin by their stages, at the LORD's command, and camped at Rephidim. And there was no water for the people to drink.

2And the people quarreled with Moses and said, "Give us water, and let us drink." And Moses said to them, "Why do you quarrel with me? Why do you test the LORD?"

3And the people thirsted there for water, and the people grumbled against Moses and said, "Why is it that you brought us up from Egypt — to kill me and my children and my livestock with thirst?"

4And Moses cried out to the LORD, saying, "What shall I do with this people? A little more and they will stone me."

5And the LORD said to Moses, "Cross over in front of the people, and take with you some of the elders of Israel. And your staff, with which you struck the Nile — take it in your hand, and go.

6Here — I will be standing before you there on the rock at Horeb. And you shall strike the rock, and water will come out of it, and the people will drink." And Moses did so before the eyes of the elders of Israel.

7And he called the name of the place Massah and Meribah, because of the quarreling of the sons of Israel, and because they tested the LORD, saying, "Is the LORD among us or not?"

Amalek at Rephidim

8And Amalek came and fought with Israel at Rephidim.

9And Moses said to Joshua, "Choose men for us, and go out, fight with Amalek. Tomorrow I will be standing on the top of the hill with the staff of God in my hand."

10And Joshua did as Moses had said to him, to fight with Amalek. And Moses, Aaron, and Hur went up to the top of the hill.

11And it was that when Moses raised his hand, Israel prevailed; and when he let his hand rest, Amalek prevailed.

12And Moses' hands were heavy. And they took a stone and put it under him, and he sat on it. And Aaron and Hur held up his hands, one on this side and one on that side. And his hands were steady until the sun went down.

13And Joshua weakened Amalek and his people by the mouth of the sword.

14And the LORD said to Moses, "Write this as a memorial in the book, and set it in the ears of Joshua: I will utterly blot out the memory of Amalek from under the heavens."

15And Moses built an altar and called its name The LORD Is My Banner.

16And he said, "For a hand upon the throne of Yah: the LORD is at war with Amalek from generation to generation."

Notes

  • v2, v7 "quarreled… tested" — the whole first half of the chapter is built out of two verbs, and the place gets named for both. Riv is not bickering; it is the word for bringing a legal case, the verb behind every courtroom scene in the prophets. Nasah is to put something to the proof. The place becomes Massah (Testing) and Meribah (Quarrel) — the names are the verbs, frozen. The Greek translators did not transliterate them the way English does. They wrote Πειρασμός and Λοιδόρησις, Testing and Reviling, so a Greek reader gets the meaning and loses the place.

  • v3 "to kill me and my children and my livestock" — the Hebrew slips into the singular mid-sentence. The people speak as a crowd in the first half of the verse and as one man in the second: my children, my cattle, my thirst. English versions usually level it to us. The text is letting a nation talk like a single frightened household.

  • v5 "your staff, with which you struck the Nile" — the verse names the staff by what it did last. That blow turned a river into blood and made water undrinkable (7:20). The same wood is now raised against a rock to make water come out. Nothing in the verse comments on this; it just makes sure the reader knows which staff.

  • v6 "I will be standing before you there on the rock" — God takes up a position on the thing that is about to be hit. The verse gives no explanation, and no later verse in Exodus returns to it.

  • v6 "before the eyes of the elders" — the Hebrew has the elders as witnesses, matching v5 where Moses is told to bring them. The Greek says he did it before the sons of Israel — the whole people watching instead of a chosen few. One of the two traditions has widened the audience.

  • v7 "Is the LORD among us or not?" — six words in Hebrew, and they are the reason the place has a name. Not did God bring us out — that is settled — but whether He is here, in the middle of the camp, today. This is the question the tabernacle occupies the last third of the book answering.

  • v9 Joshua — his first appearance, introduced without a word of explanation, as though the reader already knows him. His name is Yehoshua, the LORD saves. The Greek Old Testament spells it Ἰησοῦς — which is, letter for letter, the way the New Testament spells Jesus. They are the same name. A Greek reader met the general at Rephidim under the spelling he would later meet in the Gospels, and English gives them two different names.

  • v12 "his hands were steady" — emunah, and this is the word the rest of the Bible uses for faithfulness, the noun behind amen. Its plain sense is sitting in the open here: something that holds its position and does not give way. Faith, in the language, starts as a property of a held-up arm.

  • v14 "a memorial… the memory of Amalek" — zikkaron and zekher, the same root twice in one verse. Moses is ordered to write a permanent record of the people whose record is to be erased. The erasing is done by writing it down.

  • vv15–16 "My Banner… the throne of Yah" — nes is a pole raised where everyone can see it, a rallying signal, not a flag in the modern sense. Then v16 opens with kes, which is not the ordinary Hebrew word for throne (kisse) and occurs nowhere else in the Bible. The sentence is broken enough that the ancient translators did not read it as a throne at all: the Greek has the Lord makes war on Amalek with a hidden hand, which takes the same consonants from kasah, to cover. The Greek also renders the altar's name the Lord my refuge rather than my banner — the consonants of nes, banner, and nus, to flee for safety, are the same two letters. Two verses, and the oldest translation we have disagrees with the Hebrew on both.

chapters.title: Moses' Father-in-Law
chapters.html:
Exodus 18

Jethro Comes to the Mountain

1And Jethro, priest of Midian, Moses' father-in-law, heard all that God had done for Moses and for Israel His people, that the LORD had brought Israel out of Egypt.

2And Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, took Zipporah, Moses' wife, after her sending away,

3and her two sons — the name of the one was Gershom, for he had said, "I have been a foreigner in a foreign land,"

4and the name of the other was Eliezer, "for the God of my father was my help, and He rescued me from Pharaoh's sword" —

5and Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, came with his sons and his wife to Moses, to the wilderness where he was camped, at the mountain of God.

6And he said to Moses, "I, your father-in-law Jethro, am coming to you — and your wife, and her two sons with her."

7And Moses went out to meet his father-in-law, and bowed down and kissed him, and each asked the other how he was, and they came into the tent.

8And Moses recounted to his father-in-law everything the LORD had done to Pharaoh and to Egypt on Israel's account, all the hardship that had found them on the way, and how the LORD rescued them.

9And Jethro thrilled over all the good the LORD had done for Israel, whom He had rescued from the hand of Egypt.

10And Jethro said, "Blessed is the LORD, who rescued you from the hand of Egypt and from the hand of Pharaoh, who rescued the people from under the hand of Egypt.

11Now I know that the LORD is greater than all the gods — for in the very thing in which they acted arrogantly against them."

12And Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, took a burnt offering and sacrifices for God. And Aaron came, and all the elders of Israel, to eat bread with Moses' father-in-law before God.

The Thing Is Too Heavy for You

13And it came to pass the next day that Moses sat to judge the people, and the people stood over Moses from the morning until the evening.

14And Moses' father-in-law saw everything he was doing for the people, and said, "What is this thing you are doing for the people? Why do you sit alone, and all the people are standing over you from morning until evening?"

15And Moses said to his father-in-law, "Because the people come to me to inquire of God.

16When they have a matter, it comes to me, and I judge between a man and his neighbor, and I make known the statutes of God and His instructions."

17And Moses' father-in-law said to him, "The thing you are doing is not good.

18You will surely wither — you, and this people with you — because the thing is too heavy for you. You cannot do it alone.

19Now listen to my voice. I will advise you, and may God be with you. You be for the people in front of God, and bring the matters to God.

20And you shall warn them about the statutes and the instructions, and make known to them the way they are to walk in and the work they are to do.

21And you shall look out from all the people men of ability, who fear God, men of truth, who hate a cut taken by force — and set them over them as officers of thousands, officers of hundreds, officers of fifties, and officers of tens.

22And they shall judge the people at all times. Every great matter they shall bring to you, and every small matter they shall judge themselves. Lighten it from upon you, and let them carry it with you.

23If you do this thing, and God commands you, then you will be able to stand, and also all this people will come to its place in peace."

24And Moses listened to the voice of his father-in-law, and did all that he had said.

25And Moses chose men of ability from all Israel and made them heads over the people — officers of thousands, officers of hundreds, officers of fifties, and officers of tens.

26And they judged the people at all times. The hard matter they would bring to Moses, and every small matter they would judge themselves.

27And Moses sent his father-in-law off, and he went to his own land.

Notes

  • "Moses' father-in-law" — choten Mosheh, thirteen times in twenty-seven verses, often in the same breath as his name: Jethro, Moses' father-in-law. It is not how Hebrew narrative usually works; a named character normally keeps his name. The chapter is insisting on the relationship rather than the man, and the man it insists on is a Midianite priest.

  • v2 "after her sending away" — achar shilucheha, from shalach, the verb Moses shouted at Pharaoh in every plague: send my people away. Somewhere between chapter 4, where Zipporah is traveling to Egypt with him, and here, Moses sent his wife away. The book never tells that story. It uses the word and moves on, and then closes the chapter in v27 with the same verb again, this time for her father.

  • vv3–4 Gershom and Eliezer — both names are sentences. Ger is a resident outsider, so Gershom holds the words a foreigner there, and the verse spells it out: I have been a foreigner in a foreign land. Eliezer is my God is help, and the verse spells that out too: the God of my father was my help. Moses named his first son for exile and his second for rescue, in that order, and the two names put together are the plot of the book.

  • v9 "thrilled" — va-yichad, and the verb is so rare that its meaning has to be argued. One root gives rejoice; another gives be sharp, which in a person is the prickle that runs over the skin. The Greek translators took neither: they wrote ἐξέστη, he was beside himself, out of his mind with it. What is certain is that a strong physical reaction is meant, and that no single English word covers the range.

  • v11 "for in the very thing in which they acted arrogantly against them" — the sentence stops. There is no main clause in the Hebrew, and the Greek does not supply one either; the oldest translation is as stranded as the original. The verb is zid, to boil up and over — the root of nazid, the stew Jacob was cooking when Esau sold his birthright (Genesis 25:29). Pride in this language is a pot left on the fire.

  • v12 "and Aaron came, and all the elders of Israel" — a priest of Midian offers the sacrifice, and Israel's leadership comes to eat at his table. This is before Sinai, before Aaron is a priest, before there is a law about who may do this. The guest list is given in full and Moses is not on it.

  • v18 "you will surely wither" — navol tibbol, the verb doubled for force. It is what a leaf does on a dying branch and what a flower does in the heat — not collapse, not exhaustion, but the slow drying-out of something that was green. And the reason given is that the matter is kaved, heavy: the same word as Pharaoh's heavy heart, the LORD's heavy glory, and Moses' heavy hands six verses earlier.

  • v19 "listen to my voice" — shema be-qoli. The book uses this phrase at its hinges: the man in the garden was condemned for listening to the voice of his wife, and Abraham was commanded to listen to the voice of Sarah. Here a foreign priest says it to Moses about how to run a court, and v24 records that he did.

  • v21 "men of truth, who hate a cut taken by force" — anshe emet, from the same root as the steady hands of 17:12 — a man of emet is one who holds. And betsa is not an abstraction: the root means to cut off a piece, to break something and take your portion. It is profit pictured as a slice torn out of someone else's loaf. The Greek missed this and wrote hating arrogance.

  • v22 "and let them carry it with you" — nasa, the load verb. The whole speech treats judging as freight: too heavy for one man, lightened by dividing it, carried by others alongside him. Nothing is said about authority or rank. It is about weight.

speech.text: Exodus 18
Jethro Comes to the Mountain
And Jethro, priest of Midian, Moses' father-in-law, heard all that God had done for Moses and for Israel His people, that the LORD had brought Israel out of Egypt.
And Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, took Zipporah, Moses' wife, after her sending away,
and her two sons — the name of the one was Gershom, for he had said, "I have been a foreigner in a foreign land,"
and the name of the other was Eliezer, "for the God of my father was my help, and He rescued me from Pharaoh's sword" —
and Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, came with his sons and his wife to Moses, to the wilderness where he was camped, at the mountain of God.
And he said to Moses, "I, your father-in-law Jethro, am coming to you — and your wife, and her two sons with her."
And Moses went out to meet his father-in-law, and bowed down and kissed him, and each asked the other how he was, and they came into the tent.
And Moses recounted to his father-in-law everything the LORD had done to Pharaoh and to Egypt on Israel's account, all the hardship that had found them on the way, and how the LORD rescued them.
And Jethro thrilled over all the good the LORD had done for Israel, whom He had rescued from the hand of Egypt.
And Jethro said, "Blessed is the LORD, who rescued you from the hand of Egypt and from the hand of Pharaoh, who rescued the people from under the hand of Egypt.
Now I know that the LORD is greater than all the gods — for in the very thing in which they acted arrogantly against them."
And Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, took a burnt offering and sacrifices for God. And Aaron came, and all the elders of Israel, to eat bread with Moses' father-in-law before God.
The Thing Is Too Heavy for You
And it came to pass the next day that Moses sat to judge the people, and the people stood over Moses from the morning until the evening.

And Moses' father-in-law saw everything he was doing for the people, and said, "What is this thing you are doing for the people? Why do you sit alone, and all the people are standing over you from morning until evening?"
And Moses said to his father-in-law, "Because the people come to me to inquire of God.
When they have a matter, it comes to me, and I judge between a man and his neighbor, and I make known the statutes of God and His instructions."
And Moses' father-in-law said to him, "The thing you are doing is not good.
You will surely wither — you, and this people with you — because the thing is too heavy for you. You cannot do it alone.
Now listen to my voice. I will advise you, and may God be with you. You be for the people in front of God, and bring the matters to God.
And you shall warn them about the statutes and the instructions, and make known to them the way they are to walk in and the work they are to do.

And you shall look out from all the people men of ability, who fear God, men of truth, who hate a cut taken by force — and set them over them as officers of thousands, officers of hundreds, officers of fifties, and officers of tens.
And they shall judge the people at all times. Every great matter they shall bring to you, and every small matter they shall judge themselves. Lighten it from upon you, and let them carry it with you.
If you do this thing, and God commands you, then you will be able to stand, and also all this people will come to its place in peace."
And Moses listened to the voice of his father-in-law, and did all that he had said.
And Moses chose men of ability from all Israel and made them heads over the people — officers of thousands, officers of hundreds, officers of fifties, and officers of tens.
And they judged the people at all times. The hard matter they would bring to Moses, and every small matter they would judge themselves.
And Moses sent his father-in-law off, and he went to his own land.

chapters.title: At the Foot of the Mountain
chapters.html:
Exodus 19

A Kingdom of Priests

1In the third month of the going out of the sons of Israel from the land of Egypt, on that day they came to the wilderness of Sinai.

2And they set out from Rephidim and came to the wilderness of Sinai, and they camped in the wilderness. And Israel camped there in front of the mountain.

3And Moses went up to God, and the LORD called to him from the mountain, saying, "This is what you shall say to the house of Jacob and tell the sons of Israel:

4You yourselves have seen what I did to Egypt, and how I carried you on eagles' wings and brought you to Myself.

5And now, if you will truly listen to My voice and keep My covenant, then you will be My own treasure out of all the peoples — for all the earth is Mine.

6And you will be for Me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation. These are the words you shall speak to the sons of Israel."

7And Moses came and called the elders of the people, and set before them all these words that the LORD had commanded him.

8And all the people answered together and said, "Everything the LORD has spoken we will do." And Moses brought back the people's words to the LORD.

Set a Boundary Around the Mountain

9And the LORD said to Moses, "Here — I am coming to you in the thickness of the cloud, so that the people may hear when I speak with you, and may trust you forever as well." And Moses told the people's words to the LORD.

10And the LORD said to Moses, "Go to the people and make them holy today and tomorrow, and let them wash their clothes.

11And let them be ready for the third day, because on the third day the LORD will come down before the eyes of all the people, on Mount Sinai.

12And you shall set a boundary for the people all around, saying, 'Watch yourselves — do not go up the mountain, and do not touch its edge. Anyone who touches the mountain shall be put to death.

13No hand shall touch him: he shall be stoned or shot through — animal or man, he shall not live.' When the ram's horn sounds long, they may come up the mountain."

14And Moses went down from the mountain to the people, and made the people holy, and they washed their clothes.

15And he said to the people, "Be ready for three days. Do not go near a woman."

The Third Day

16And it came to pass on the third day, when it was morning, that there were thunders and lightnings, and a heavy cloud on the mountain, and the sound of a horn, very strong. And all the people in the camp trembled.

17And Moses brought the people out of the camp to meet God, and they took their stand at the foot of the mountain.

18And Mount Sinai was smoking, all of it, because the LORD had come down on it in fire. And its smoke went up like the smoke of a kiln, and the whole mountain trembled violently.

19And the sound of the horn went on and grew very strong. Moses would speak, and God would answer him in a voice.

20And the LORD came down on Mount Sinai, to the top of the mountain. And the LORD called Moses to the top of the mountain, and Moses went up.

21And the LORD said to Moses, "Go down, warn the people — or they will break through to the LORD to look, and many of them will fall.

22And the priests too, who come near to the LORD, must make themselves holy, or the LORD will break out against them."

23And Moses said to the LORD, "The people cannot come up Mount Sinai, because You Yourself warned us, saying, 'Set a boundary around the mountain and make it holy.'"

24And the LORD said to him, "Go down, and come back up — you, and Aaron with you. But the priests and the people must not break through to come up to the LORD, or He will break out against them."

25And Moses went down to the people, and said to them —

Notes

  • v2 "and Israel camped there" — the verse uses the verb twice, and changes number between them. They camped in the wilderness, plural, the way the book has said it at every stop since Egypt; then Israel camped in front of the mountain, singular, one subject with one verb. A crowd arrives in the wilderness and a nation arrives at the mountain, and the whole change is a letter.

  • v4 "on eagles' wings" — nesher. The bird is not certainly an eagle: the word is used of a carrion bird that goes bald (Micah 1:16), which fits the griffon vulture, the great soaring scavenger of that country, better than any eagle. Both are enormous, both ride the thermals without beating a wing. The picture the Hebrew reaches for is the carrying, not the species, and English has quietly chosen the nobler bird.

  • v5 "My own treasure" — segullah, and it is not a poetic word. It is the term for a king's private wealth, the hoard that is his personally and not the crown's, kept separate from the treasury he administers. God has just said all the earth is Mine — the whole estate — and then sets one people aside as the thing He owns the other way.

  • v6 "a holy nation" — goy qadosh. Israel is almost always am, a people; goy is the standard word for everybody else, the nations. Here, at the moment of the covenant, the book calls Israel a goy — the same category as everyone it will spend the rest of the canon being distinguished from, with one adjective doing all the work.

  • v8 "Everything the LORD has spoken we will do" — na'aseh. The Greek translators had a text that said more: we will do and we will hear. That fuller form is the famous one, and in the Hebrew it does not appear until 24:7. Whether the Greek anticipated it or the Hebrew dropped it, the two oldest witnesses disagree about what Israel said when it agreed.

  • v9 "in the thickness of the cloud" — av, a dense mass of cloud, the word for weather that has body to it. The Greek reads in a pillar of cloud, importing the column that led them out of Egypt. The Hebrew is not describing a shape; it is describing opacity. God comes in the part of the cloud you cannot see into.

  • v13 "when the ram's horn sounds long, they may come up" — after two verses of absolute prohibition, the same sentence ends by granting exactly what it forbade, and nothing in the chapter explains the signal or reports it being given. The horn is yovel — the word that names the Jubilee, the fiftieth year announced by blowing it. The Greek has a different text here entirely: when the voices and the trumpets and the cloud depart from the mountain, then they may go up.

  • v15 "Do not go near a woman" — God told Moses two things in vv10–11: make them holy, wash their clothes. Moses relays both in v14 and then adds a third that he was not given. The text reports the addition without comment, and every later reader who has taken this as God's requirement is quoting Moses.

  • vv16, 18 "trembled" — charad, the verb for the shudder that goes through a body. In v16 it is the people who tremble; in v18 the Hebrew says the whole mountain trembled. The Greek says the people did, both times. One letter separates ha-am, the people, from ha-har, the mountain, and the two traditions took it different ways — leaving a real question about whether the mountain in this chapter is shaking or only the crowd at the bottom of it.

  • vv21–24 "break through… break out" — two different verbs, aimed in opposite directions. Haras is what you do to a wall: tear it down, demolish it. Parats is to burst a breach and come pouring through. The people are warned not to demolish the boundary from below, and the danger named is that God will burst out of it from above. The barrier is described as holding back pressure on both sides.

  • v25 "and said to them —" — the chapter stops mid-sentence. Moses goes down and opens his mouth and the verse ends; the next words in the book are God's, beginning the Ten Commandments. The speech Moses was about to give is never recorded.

chapters.title: The Ten Words
chapters.html:
Exodus 20

The Ten Words

1And God spoke all these words, saying:

2"I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slaves.

3You shall have no other gods before My face.

4You shall not make for yourself a carved image, or any form of what is in the heavens above, or on the earth below, or in the waters under the earth.

5You shall not bow down to them and you shall not serve them — because I, the LORD your God, am a jealous God, calling the guilt of fathers to account on sons, on the third and on the fourth generation of those who hate Me,

6and doing loyal love to thousands, for those who love Me and keep My commandments.

7You shall not lift up the name of the LORD your God for emptiness, because the LORD will not leave unpunished the one who lifts up His name for emptiness.

8Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy.

9Six days you shall work and do all your labor,

10and the seventh day is a sabbath to the LORD your God. You shall not do any labor — you, or your son, or your daughter, your male slave or your female slave, or your animal, or the foreigner who is inside your gates.

11For in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth, the sea and everything in them, and He rested on the seventh day. Therefore the LORD blessed the sabbath day and made it holy.

12Honor your father and your mother, so that your days may be long on the ground that the LORD your God is giving you.

13You shall not murder.

14You shall not commit adultery.

15You shall not steal.

16You shall not answer against your neighbor as a false witness.

17You shall not covet your neighbor's house. You shall not covet your neighbor's wife, or his male slave, or his female slave, or his ox, or his donkey, or anything that is your neighbor's."

Do Not Let God Speak With Us

18And all the people were seeing the thunders and the torches and the sound of the horn and the mountain smoking. And the people saw, and they shook, and they stood far off.

19And they said to Moses, "You speak with us, and we will listen. But do not let God speak with us, or we will die."

20And Moses said to the people, "Do not be afraid, because God has come in order to test you, and so that the fear of Him will be on your faces, so that you do not sin."

21And the people stood far off, and Moses drew near to the thick darkness where God was.

An Altar of Earth

22And the LORD said to Moses, "This is what you shall say to the sons of Israel: You yourselves have seen that I spoke with you from the heavens.

23You shall not make gods of silver alongside Me, and gods of gold you shall not make for yourselves.

24An altar of earth you shall make for Me, and you shall sacrifice on it your burnt offerings and your peace offerings, your flock and your herd. In every place where I cause My name to be remembered, I will come to you and bless you.

25And if you make Me an altar of stones, you shall not build them cut — because you have waved your sword over it and profaned it.

26And you shall not go up by steps onto My altar, so that your nakedness is not uncovered on it."

Notes

  • v1 "all these words" — the text does not call them commandments. It calls them devarim, words, and 34:28 names them exactly: the ten words, which the Greek renders tous deka logous — the source of Decalogue. English gained "the Ten Commandments" from the Latin tradition; neither original language says command anywhere in the title.

  • v3 "before My face" — al panai, and the preposition is genuinely open. It can mean in My presence, in preference to Me, in front of Me as a rival stands in front of a rival, or simply besides Me. Each reading forbids something slightly different, and the Hebrew does not choose. The Greek chose: except Me.

  • v5 "a jealous God… calling to account" — qanna is the word for a husband's jealousy over his wife, not for envy of a stranger's goods; it is possessive, and it belongs to a relationship that already exists. And poqed is the wide verb from Genesis 21:1, where the LORD attended to Sarah — to muster, to number, to call in what is owed. Guilt is being counted, the way a commander counts troops.

  • v6 "loyal love to thousands" — the two halves of the sentence are not the same size. Guilt reaches the third and fourth generation; chesed reaches thousands — and the Hebrew does not say thousands of what, so it may be thousands of people or thousands of generations. Either way the asymmetry is the point, and it is deliberate enough that Deuteronomy repeats it word for word.

  • v7 "lift up the name… for emptiness" — nasa, to pick up and carry, the same verb as carrying a load or bearing guilt. This is not primarily about swearing in the sense of cursing. It is about taking the name up onto yourself — swearing by it, invoking it, acting in it — when what you are carrying it for is shav: emptiness, worthlessness, a thing with nothing inside it. An oath kept is the name well carried; an oath broken is the name carried for nothing.

  • v12 "Honor" — kabbed, the causative of heavy. Literally: make your father and mother weigh something. The same root has run through Exodus as Pharaoh's hardened heart, the LORD's glory, Moses' tired hands, and the burden of judging that was too heavy for one man. Here it becomes a command, and its opposite in Hebrew is not disrespect but qalal, to treat as light.

  • v13 "murder" — ratsach, and it is not the general word for killing. Hebrew has harag and hemit for that, and uses them for war, for execution, for God putting someone to death. Ratsach is the word the law uses for the killings that send a man to a city of refuge — unlawful killing, including by accident. The commandment is narrower than "do not kill" and the language marks the difference.

  • vv13–15 the order is not fixed — the Hebrew runs murder, adultery, theft. The Greek Old Testament runs adultery, theft, murder. This is not a scribal slip; it is how the oldest translation of Exodus reads. And when the New Testament quotes the list — Luke 18:20, Romans 13:9, James 2:11 — adultery comes first every time, following the Greek against the Hebrew. Three writers in three different books, all reciting the Ten Commandments in an order most English readers have never heard.

  • v17 the last commandment is longer in Greek — the Hebrew forbids coveting the house first and the wife second. The Greek reverses them, putting the wife first, and adds a possession the Hebrew does not list: his field. Deuteronomy's Hebrew version also puts the wife first. The three witnesses agree on what is forbidden and disagree on what comes first in a man's inventory.

  • v18 "the people were seeing the thunders" — qolot means thunders and voices with the same word, and the verb is seeing. The Greek did not tidy it either: the people saw the voice. Both traditions kept a sentence in which sound is something you look at.

  • v25 "you have waved your sword over it" — the word is cherev, sword, not chisel, and it is the ordinary word for the weapon. The reason dressed stone profanes an altar is given in the tool's name: the thing that shapes the block is the thing that kills a man. An altar is to be made of earth, or of stones nobody has touched with a blade.

chapters.title: And These Are the Rulings
chapters.html:
Exodus 21

1And these are the rulings that you shall set before them.

Slaves

2When you buy a Hebrew slave, he shall serve six years, and in the seventh he shall go out free, for nothing.

3If he came in by himself, he shall go out by himself. If he was the husband of a wife, then his wife shall go out with him.

4If his master gives him a wife and she bears him sons or daughters, the wife and her children shall belong to her master, and he shall go out by himself.

5And if the slave says plainly, "I love my master, my wife, and my sons — I will not go out free,"

6then his master shall bring him to God, and shall bring him to the door or to the doorpost, and his master shall pierce his ear with an awl, and he shall serve him for life.

7And when a man sells his daughter as a slave woman, she shall not go out as the male slaves go out.

8If she is displeasing in the eyes of her master, who designated her for himself, he shall let her be redeemed. He has no right to sell her to a foreign people, since he has broken faith with her.

9And if he designates her for his son, he shall do for her according to the ruling for daughters.

10If he takes another for himself, he shall not withhold from her her food, her clothing, or her due.

11And if he does not do these three things for her, she shall go out for nothing, without payment.

Capital Cases

12Whoever strikes a man so that he dies shall be put to death.

13But if he did not lie in wait, and God let it meet his hand, then I will appoint for you a place where he may flee.

14And when a man acts with intent against his neighbor, to kill him by cunning, you shall take him from My altar to die.

15And whoever strikes his father or his mother shall be put to death.

16And whoever steals a man and sells him, or he is found in his hand, shall be put to death.

17And whoever curses his father or his mother shall be put to death.

Injury

18And when men quarrel and one strikes his neighbor with a stone or with a fist, and he does not die but takes to his bed —

19if he gets up and walks about outside on his staff, the one who struck him shall be clear. Only he shall pay for his sitting still, and shall pay for his healing.

20And when a man strikes his male slave or his female slave with a rod, and the slave dies under his hand, it shall be avenged.

21But if the slave stands up after a day or two, it shall not be avenged, for he is his money.

22And when two men fight and strike a pregnant woman, and her child comes out not yet formed, he shall be fined. As the woman's husband imposes on him, so he shall pay, by assessment.

23But if it was formed, he shall give life for life,

24eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot,

25burn for burn, wound for wound, bruise for bruise.

26And when a man strikes the eye of his male slave or the eye of his female slave and ruins it, he shall let the slave go free in place of the eye.

27And if he knocks out the tooth of his male slave or the tooth of his female slave, he shall let the slave go free in place of the tooth.

The Goring Ox and the Open Pit

28And when an ox gores a man or a woman so that they die, the ox shall be stoned and its flesh shall not be eaten, and the owner of the ox is clear.

29But if the ox was a gorer from yesterday and the day before, and its owner was warned and did not keep it in, and it kills a man or a woman, the ox shall be stoned and its owner also shall be put to death.

30If a ransom is imposed on him, he shall give the redemption of his life according to all that is imposed on him.

31Whether it gores a son or gores a daughter, this same ruling shall be done for him.

32If the ox gores a male slave or a female slave, he shall give thirty shekels of silver to their master, and the ox shall be stoned.

33And when a man opens a pit, or when a man digs a pit and does not cover it, and an ox or a donkey falls into it,

34the owner of the pit shall make it good. He shall return silver to its owner, and the dead animal shall be his.

35And when one man's ox strikes his neighbor's ox and it dies, they shall sell the live ox and divide the silver, and they shall also divide the dead one.

36Or if it was known that the ox was a gorer from yesterday and the day before, and its owner did not keep it in, he shall make good, ox for ox, and the dead one shall be his.

Notes

  • v1 "the rulings" — mishpatim, from shafat, to judge. Not commandments and not statutes: decisions, the kind a court hands down. And the whole chapter is built on one sentence shape — when such a thing happens, then this is done — which is how a case is written up rather than how a rule is proclaimed. Chapter 20 said you shall not. Chapter 21 says when a man's ox gores. The two are different kinds of writing sitting back to back.

  • v3 "by himself" — be-gappo, a word that occurs in the Hebrew Bible only here and in v4, twice in the same law. Something like with his body only — he arrived with nothing and leaves with nothing. Because nothing else in the language uses it, its exact force cannot be recovered; what the law does with it is clear enough, and brutal: v4 says a wife given to him by the master stays behind, and so do his children.

  • v6 "bring him to God… pierce his ear" — ha-elohim, which can be God or the divine court, and the Greek settled it one way: to the judgment-seat of God. Then the man is put against the door, and the awl goes through his ear into the doorpost he will keep going through. And the term is le-olam, the word for the farthest horizon anyone can see — the same word in El Olam, God of Everlasting, at Genesis 21:33. Here it means: until you die.

  • v10 "her food, her clothing, or her due" — the third item is onatah, and nobody can say for certain what it is. Proposals run from her conjugal right, to oil, to lodging, to her time — each argued from a different root, none decisive. What the law is doing is not in doubt: a man who takes a second wife owes the first three specific things, and v11 says failing any one of them buys her freedom outright. The obscure word is one of the three.

  • vv13–14 "God let it meet his hand… take him from My altar" — the line between murder and accident is drawn twice and from both sides. On one side, an unintended killing is described as something God caused to meet the man's hand, and the Greek says the same: God delivered it into his hands. On the other, a man who killed be-ormah, by cunning, gets no refuge: the altar is named as the place he will be dragged away from. Holy ground shelters the one and not the other, and the difference is entirely what was in his head.

  • v16 "whoever steals a man" — kidnapping carries the same sentence as murder, and the law is stated with no qualification. Set it against the end of this chapter: stealing an ox costs five oxen. Stealing a person costs your life.

  • vv20–21 "for he is his money" — ki khaspo hu. The law limits what an owner may do — kill a slave with a rod and it shall be avenged — and then says that if the slave survives a day or two there is no case, and gives the reason in three words. Both halves are in the same paragraph. The verse restrains the owner and prices the slave in the same breath, and no English rendering can make that read comfortably.

  • vv22–23 the two witnesses ask different questions — this rendering follows the Greek, and the two oldest texts of Exodus do not set the same test.

    The Greek turns on exeikonismenon, from eikōn, image or shape: the child comes out mē exeikonismenon, not yet formed, and the penalty is money; but if it was formed, the penalty is psychēn anti psychēs, life for life. That is a threshold, and it is a threshold a court could actually work: nobody in this world counts weeks, so the standard is read off the body — you look at what came out and see whether it had taken human shape. Neither verse contains a word for dying. It says only that the child came out, and in a world without any means of keeping a premature infant alive, a pregnancy that comes out early does not survive. What the Greek grades, then, is how far along the lost child had come.

    The Hebrew does not grade it. Its condition is ason, harm — no ason, a fine; ason, life for life — and it never says whose harm. If the children coming out is itself the loss, then the no-ason case is the dead child and a fine covers it, which leaves ason to mean harm to the woman. Read that way the Hebrew sets no threshold at all: the pregnancy is compensable at any stage, and only the woman is life for life. Ason is rare enough that nothing in the verse settles it; what fixes its weight is elsewhere in this canon, where it is the word Jacob keeps using about Benjamin — harm might come to him (Genesis 42:4, 42:38, 44:29).

    One asks how developed the child was. The other asks who got hurt. Neither is a version of the other, and both sit inside a chapter about what one man owes another when a fight goes wrong — the fine is set by the woman's husband, and paid to him.

  • vv24–27 "eye for eye" — seven pairs run on the preposition tachat, in place of, in two verses, and the famous phrase is not a general principle here. It sits inside a single case about a fight and a miscarriage, and it caps what may be exacted rather than licensing it. Then the next two verses reuse the identical formula to a different end: an owner who destroys a slave's eye lets the slave go free in place of the eye. The compensation clause has become an emancipation clause with the same three words.

  • v32 "thirty shekels of silver" — the fixed sum an ox's owner pays when the ox kills someone else's slave. It is the only place the law puts an exact price on a human being. The Greek writes it thirty pieces of silver — τριάκοντα, ἀργυρίου — and that is the figure the chief priests weigh out to Judas in Matthew 26:15: thirty pieces of silver, τριάκοντα ἀργύρια. The amount is not invented for the Gospel; it is the compensation this chapter sets for a dead slave.

speech.text: Exodus 21
And these are the rulings that you shall set before them.
Slaves
When you buy a Hebrew slave, he shall serve six years, and in the seventh he shall go out free, for nothing.
If he came in by himself, he shall go out by himself. If he was the husband of a wife, then his wife shall go out with him.
If his master gives him a wife and she bears him sons or daughters, the wife and her children shall belong to her master, and he shall go out by himself.
And if the slave says plainly, "I love my master, my wife, and my sons — I will not go out free,"
then his master shall bring him to God, and shall bring him to the door or to the doorpost, and his master shall pierce his ear with an awl, and he shall serve him for life.
And when a man sells his daughter as a slave woman, she shall not go out as the male slaves go out.
If she is displeasing in the eyes of her master, who designated her for himself, he shall let her be redeemed. He has no right to sell her to a foreign people, since he has broken faith with her.
And if he designates her for his son, he shall do for her according to the ruling for daughters.
If he takes another for himself, he shall not withhold from her her food, her clothing, or her due.
And if he does not do these three things for her, she shall go out for nothing, without payment.
Capital Cases
Whoever strikes a man so that he dies shall be put to death.
But if he did not lie in wait, and God let it meet his hand, then I will appoint for you a place where he may flee.
And when a man acts with intent against his neighbor, to kill him by cunning, you shall take him from My altar to die.
And whoever strikes his father or his mother shall be put to death.
And whoever steals a man and sells him, or he is found in his hand, shall be put to death.
And whoever curses his father or his mother shall be put to death.
Injury
And when men quarrel and one strikes his neighbor with a stone or with a fist, and he does not die but takes to his bed —
if he gets up and walks about outside on his staff, the one who struck him shall be clear. Only he shall pay for his sitting still, and shall pay for his healing.
And when a man strikes his male slave or his female slave with a rod, and the slave dies under his hand, it shall be avenged.
But if the slave stands up after a day or two, it shall not be avenged, for he is his money.
And when two men fight and strike a pregnant woman, and her child comes out not yet formed, he shall be fined. As the woman's husband imposes on him, so he shall pay, by assessment.
But if it was formed, he shall give life for life,
eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot,
burn for burn, wound for wound, bruise for bruise.
And when a man strikes the eye of his male slave or the eye of his female slave and ruins it, he shall let the slave go free in place of the eye.
And if he knocks out the tooth of his male slave or the tooth of his female slave, he shall let the slave go free in place of the tooth.
The Goring Ox and the Open Pit
And when an ox gores a man or a woman so that they die, the ox shall be stoned and its flesh shall not be eaten, and the owner of the ox is clear.

But if the ox was a gorer from yesterday and the day before, and its owner was warned and did not keep it in, and it kills a man or a woman, the ox shall be stoned and its owner also shall be put to death.
If a ransom is imposed on him, he shall give the redemption of his life according to all that is imposed on him.
Whether it gores a son or gores a daughter, this same ruling shall be done for him.
If the ox gores a male slave or a female slave, he shall give thirty shekels of silver to their master, and the ox shall be stoned.
And when a man opens a pit, or when a man digs a pit and does not cover it, and an ox or a donkey falls into it,
the owner of the pit shall make it good. He shall return silver to its owner, and the dead animal shall be his.
And when one man's ox strikes his neighbor's ox and it dies, they shall sell the live ox and divide the silver, and they shall also divide the dead one.
Or if it was known that the ox was a gorer from yesterday and the day before, and its owner did not keep it in, he shall make good, ox for ox, and the dead one shall be his.

chapters.title: When a Man Steals
chapters.html:
Exodus 22

Restitution

1When a man steals an ox or a sheep and slaughters it or sells it, he shall pay five oxen in place of the ox and four sheep in place of the sheep.

2If the thief is found breaking in and is struck so that he dies, there is no bloodguilt for him.

3If the sun has risen on him, there is bloodguilt. He shall make full payment; and if he has nothing, he shall be sold for his theft.

4If the stolen thing is found in his hand alive — from ox to donkey to sheep — he shall pay double.

5When a man grazes a field or a vineyard, and sends his beast out and it grazes in another man's field, he shall make it good from the best of his own field and the best of his own vineyard.

6When fire breaks out and catches in thorns, and a stack of grain or the standing grain or the field is consumed, the one who started the fire shall make full payment.

7When a man gives his neighbor silver or goods to keep, and it is stolen from the man's house — if the thief is found, he shall pay double.

8If the thief is not found, then the owner of the house shall be brought to God, to swear that he did not put his hand to his neighbor's property.

9In every case of breach of trust — over an ox, over a donkey, over a sheep, over a garment, over anything lost, of which one says, "This is it" — the matter of them both shall come before God. Whomever God declares guilty shall pay double to his neighbor.

10When a man gives his neighbor a donkey or an ox or a sheep or any animal to keep, and it dies or is injured or is driven off, with no one seeing,

11an oath by the LORD shall be between the two of them, that he did not put his hand to his neighbor's property. And the owner shall accept it, and he shall not pay.

12But if it was stolen from him, he shall pay its owner.

13If it was torn by a beast, he shall bring it as evidence; he shall not pay for what was torn.

14And when a man borrows from his neighbor and it is injured or dies, its owner not being with it, he shall make full payment.

15If its owner was with it, he shall not pay. If it was hired, it comes at its hire.

Things Not Tolerated

16And when a man seduces a young woman who is not promised in marriage, and lies with her, he shall pay the bride-price for her, as his wife.

17If her father utterly refuses to give her to him, he shall weigh out silver according to the bride-price of young women.

18A sorceress you shall not let live.

19Whoever lies with an animal shall be put to death.

20Whoever sacrifices to gods, except to the LORD alone, shall be devoted to destruction.

The Foreigner, the Widow, the Poor

21And you shall not wrong a foreigner and you shall not press him down, for you were foreigners in the land of Egypt.

22You shall not afflict any widow or orphan.

23If you do afflict him — if he cries out to Me, I will surely hear his cry,

24and My anger will burn, and I will kill you with the sword, and your wives will become widows and your children orphans.

25If you lend silver to My people, to the poor among you, you shall not be a creditor to him. You shall not lay interest on him.

26If you take your neighbor's cloak as a pledge, you shall return it to him before the sun goes down,

27because it is his only covering — it is his garment for his skin. In what shall he sleep? And when he cries out to Me, I will hear, for I am gracious.

What Is Owed to God

28You shall not curse God, and you shall not curse a leader among your people.

29You shall not delay your full harvest or your outflow. The firstborn of your sons you shall give to Me.

30So you shall do with your ox and with your flock: seven days it shall be with its mother, and on the eighth day you shall give it to Me.

31And you shall be men of holiness to Me. And flesh torn in the field you shall not eat; you shall throw it to the dog.

Notes

  • v1 the chapter starts a verse earlier in Hebrew — this law is numbered 21:37 in the Hebrew Bible, so the whole of Hebrew chapter 22 runs one verse behind this one. The Greek agrees with the English. Anyone reading this alongside a Hebrew text should expect the offset from here to the end of the chapter.

  • vv2–3 "there is no bloodguilt… there is bloodguilt" — damim, blood in the plural, which in Hebrew means liability for blood rather than the substance. The right to kill a housebreaker lasts exactly as long as the dark: if the sun has risen on him, the same blow is murder. What changes is not the threat but whether the householder could see who he was hitting.

  • vv8–9 "brought to God… whomever God declares guilty" — ha-elohim again, as in 21:6, and here the procedure is spelled out: where there is no thief and no witness, the case goes to the sanctuary and a man swears. The Greek keeps it as God — before God — rather than resolving it into human judges. A property dispute with no evidence is settled by an oath nobody can check, which is the point: the only remaining witness is the one being sworn to.

  • vv16–17 "the bride-price" — mohar, the sum a man paid a bride's family. The law gives the father a veto and leaves the payment standing either way: he may refuse the marriage and still collect the full amount. The woman's own wishes are not part of the ruling.

  • v18 "a sorceress" — mekhashefah, and the Hebrew is feminine singular. Every other capital law in this stretch is put in the masculine or in a form covering anyone; this one names a woman. The masculine form of the word exists and is used elsewhere in the canon. It is not used here.

  • v21 "for you were foreigners in the land of Egypt" — ger, a resident outsider, the word this rendering refuses to translate as sojourner. The commandment does not argue from principle or from the foreigner's rights. It argues from memory: you know what this feels like from the inside. It is the only reason given, and the book will give it again.

  • vv23–24 "your wives will become widows and your children orphans" — the sentence is the crime handed back. Afflict a widow and an orphan, and the punishment named is that your own household becomes widows and orphans. Nothing else in this chapter is framed that way; every other penalty is payment, death, or destruction.

  • vv26–27 "In what shall he sleep?" — a rhetorical question, in the middle of a statute. The law is about a poor man's cloak taken as security on a loan, and instead of stating a rule it asks what the man is supposed to do at night, then says God will hear him if he cries out, ki chanun ani — for I am gracious. A legal code stops to picture one cold man and gives God's character as the enforcement.

  • v28 "You shall not curse God, and… a leader" — elohim and nasi, and the Greek read the first word as a plural: Θεούς, gods. Paul quotes the second half in Greek at his trial — you shall not speak evil of a ruler of your people (Acts 23:5) — in the Septuagint's wording rather than the Hebrew's, after insulting the high priest and being told who he was.

  • v29 "your outflow… the firstborn of your sons" — dim'akha, and the ordinary meaning of dim'a is a tear, the kind you weep; here it has to mean the juice that runs from a press, wine or oil. The word for what comes out of an eye is the word for what comes out of crushed fruit. Then the verse turns without a pause to firstborn sons, and — unlike 13:13, which says every firstborn of man among your sons you shall redeem — says nothing about redemption. The book carries both sentences and does not reconcile them here.

chapters.title: My Name Is Within Him
chapters.html:
Exodus 23

In Court

1You shall not lift up an empty report. You shall not put your hand in with a guilty man to be a violent witness.

2You shall not follow the crowd into wrong, and you shall not testify in a dispute so as to side with the crowd and pervert justice.

3And you shall not favor a poor man in his dispute.

4When you come upon your enemy's ox or his donkey wandering, you shall surely bring it back to him.

5When you see the donkey of the one who hates you lying down under its load, do not hold back from him — you shall surely help him with it.

6You shall not turn aside the judgment of your needy in his dispute.

7Keep far from a false charge. And do not kill the innocent and the righteous, for I will not acquit the guilty.

8And you shall not take a bribe, because a bribe blinds the clear-sighted and twists the words of the righteous.

9And you shall not press down a foreigner, for you yourselves know the soul of the foreigner — because you were foreigners in the land of Egypt.

The Seventh

10And six years you shall sow your land and gather in its produce.

11And the seventh you shall let go and leave it, and the needy of your people shall eat, and what they leave the beast of the field shall eat. So you shall do with your vineyard and with your olive grove.

12Six days you shall do your work, and on the seventh day you shall stop — so that your ox and your donkey may rest, and the son of your slave woman and the foreigner may draw breath.

13And in all that I have said to you, be watchful. And the name of other gods you shall not mention; it shall not be heard on your mouth.

Three Times in the Year

14Three times in the year you shall hold a festival to Me.

15The Festival of Unleavened Bread you shall keep. Seven days you shall eat unleavened bread, as I commanded you, at the appointed time of the month of Abib, because in it you came out of Egypt. And they shall not appear before My face empty-handed.

16And the Festival of the Harvest, the firstfruits of your work that you sow in the field. And the Festival of the Gathering, at the going out of the year, when you gather in your work from the field.

17Three times in the year all your males shall appear before the face of the Lord, the LORD.

18You shall not offer the blood of My sacrifice with anything leavened, and the fat of My festival shall not stay the night until morning.

19The first of the firstfruits of your ground you shall bring to the house of the LORD your God. You shall not boil a young goat in its mother's milk.

The Messenger Before You

20Here — I am sending a messenger before you, to guard you on the way and to bring you to the place I have prepared.

21Be watchful before him and listen to his voice. Do not rebel against him, for he will not bear your transgression, because My name is within him.

22But if you truly listen to his voice and do all that I speak, then I will be an enemy to your enemies and an adversary to your adversaries.

23For My messenger will go before you and bring you to the Amorite and the Hittite and the Perizzite and the Canaanite, the Hivite and the Jebusite, and I will wipe them out.

24You shall not bow down to their gods and you shall not serve them, and you shall not do as they do. You shall utterly tear them down and utterly break their standing stones.

25And you shall serve the LORD your God, and He will bless your bread and your water, and I will take sickness away from among you.

26There shall be no woman miscarrying or barren in your land. I will fill out the number of your days.

27I will send My terror before you and throw into confusion every people you come among, and I will make all your enemies turn their backs to you.

28And I will send the hornet before you, and it shall drive out the Hivite, the Canaanite and the Hittite from before you.

29I will not drive them out from before you in one year, or the land would become desolate and the beast of the field multiply against you.

30Little by little I will drive them out from before you, until you are fruitful and take the land as your possession.

31And I will set your border from the Sea of Reeds to the Sea of the Philistines, and from the wilderness to the River. For I will give the inhabitants of the land into your hand, and you shall drive them out from before you.

32You shall not cut a covenant with them or with their gods.

33They shall not live in your land, or they will make you sin against Me — for you would serve their gods, and it would become a snare to you.

Notes

  • v1 "lift up an empty report" — lo tissa shema shav, and the third commandment three chapters back was lo tissa et shem… la-shav, you shall not lift up the name for emptiness (20:7). Same verb, same noun shav; the only difference is shem, name, against shema, a thing heard — one letter apart in Hebrew. Swearing falsely by God and spreading a rumor are written as the same act performed on different objects.

  • vv3, 6 "you shall not favor a poor man… you shall not turn aside the judgment of your needy" — both, three verses apart. The court is told not to tilt against the poor man and not to tilt toward him either. The second is the one no English reader expects, and it is the reason the first is not charity: what is being protected is the judgment, not the party.

  • v5 "do not hold back from him — you shall surely help him with it" — the verb is azav, which everywhere else means to leave, abandon, let go, and it appears here twice with opposite force required by the sentence: you must not azav him, you must surely azav with him. Either it carries a second sense of loosing a load that survives nowhere else, or the text is damaged. What the law wants is plain regardless, and it is aimed at an enemy: his animal is down, and you are the one who has to get under it with him.

  • v9 "you know the soul of the foreigner" — the second time in two chapters that the Egypt memory is given as the reason (22:21), and this one adds nefesh ha-ger: not his situation, his soul — the inside of it. The law assumes its readers still have that knowledge available and can be argued with from it.

  • v11 "you shall let it go" — tishmetennah, from shamat, to drop or release something you are holding. It is the root behind shemittah, the name the seventh year eventually carried. And the beneficiaries are named in order: the needy of your people first, and whatever they leave, wild animals. The land's rest is legislated as somebody else's food.

  • v12 "may draw breath" — yinnafesh, a verb built on nefesh, throat and breath and life. The sabbath command here gives no reason about creation and no reason about Egypt: the reason is that the ox, the donkey, the slave woman's son and the foreigner get to breathe. The one person whose rest is not mentioned is the man being commanded.

  • v13 "it shall not be heard on your mouth" — not do not worship them: do not say the names. The prohibition is on the sound, and the phrasing puts the hearing in someone else's ear — a name is not to be heard coming off your lips.

  • v14 "three times" — shalosh regalim, and regel is a foot. Three footings in the year, three times the whole body has to get up and go somewhere. Hebrew counts these festivals by the walking they require, which is why they are pilgrim feasts, and English "times" loses the legs entirely.

  • v19 "you shall not boil a young goat in its mother's milk" — stated three times in the Torah and never once explained: here, at 34:26, and at Deuteronomy 14:21. No reason, no penalty, no context — at 34:26 it again follows the firstfruits, and at Deuteronomy it follows a rule about carrion. The entire separation of meat from dairy in later Jewish practice rests on a sentence the text gives no argument for.

  • v21 "My name is within him" — ki shemi be-qirbo. The messenger must be obeyed, cannot forgive, and carries the name inside him. Nothing in Exodus explains what that means, and the chapter moves straight on to boundaries and battle plans. Set beside 33:2–3, where God offers to send a messenger instead of going Himself and Moses refuses, the sentence becomes the question the rest of the book argues about: whether a messenger with the name in him is the same as God going along.

  • v28 "the hornet" — tzir'ah, a word that occurs three times in the Hebrew Bible and all three are this same promise about clearing the land (here, Deuteronomy 7:20, Joshua 24:12). Because it never appears in an ordinary sentence, nothing fixes its meaning: a stinging insect is the traditional reading, and a plague or a terror that goes ahead of an army has been argued from the same letters. The one thing the word always does is drive people out.

  • vv29–30 "little by little" — me'at me'at. The reason given for the slowness is ecological rather than moral: clear the land too fast and it goes to waste, and the wild animals take it over. The conquest is paced to how quickly one nation can actually farm.

The first of the firstfruits of your ground you shall bring to the house of the LORD your God. You shall not boil a young goat in its mother's milk.
The Messenger Before You
Here — I am sending a messenger before you, to guard you on the way and to bring you to the place I have prepared.
Be watchful before him and listen to his voice. Do not rebel against him, for he will not bear your transgression, because My name is within him.
But if you truly listen to his voice and do all that I speak, then I will be an enemy to your enemies and an adversary to your adversaries.
For My messenger will go before you and bring you to the Amorite and the Hittite and the Perizzite and the Canaanite, the Hivite and the Jebusite, and I will wipe them out.
You shall not bow down to their gods and you shall not serve them, and you shall not do as they do. You shall utterly tear them down and utterly break their standing stones.
And you shall serve the LORD your God, and He will bless your bread and your water, and I will take sickness away from among you.
There shall be no woman miscarrying or barren in your land. I will fill out the number of your days.
I will send My terror before you and throw into confusion every people you come among, and I will make all your enemies turn their backs to you.
And I will send the hornet before you, and it shall drive out the Hivite, the Canaanite and the Hittite from before you.
I will not drive them out from before you in one year, or the land would become desolate and the beast of the field multiply against you.
Little by little I will drive them out from before you, until you are fruitful and take the land as your possession.

And I will set your border from the Sea of Reeds to the Sea of the Philistines, and from the wilderness to the River. For I will give the inhabitants of the land into your hand, and you shall drive them out from before you.
You shall not cut a covenant with them or with their gods.
They shall not live in your land, or they will make you sin against Me — for you would serve their gods, and it would become a snare to you.

chapters.title: The Blood of the Covenant
chapters.html:
Exodus 24

All the Words We Will Do

1And to Moses He said, "Go up to the LORD — you and Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel — and bow down from a distance.

2And Moses alone shall come near to the LORD. They shall not come near, and the people shall not go up with him."

3And Moses came and recounted to the people all the words of the LORD and all the rulings. And all the people answered with one voice and said, "All the words the LORD has spoken we will do."

4And Moses wrote down all the words of the LORD. And he rose early in the morning and built an altar at the foot of the mountain, and twelve standing stones for the twelve tribes of Israel.

5And he sent the young men of the sons of Israel, and they offered burnt offerings and sacrificed bulls as peace offerings to the LORD.

6And Moses took half the blood and put it in basins, and half the blood he threw against the altar.

7And he took the book of the covenant and read it in the ears of the people. And they said, "All that the LORD has spoken we will do, and we will listen."

8And Moses took the blood and threw it on the people, and said, "Here — the blood of the covenant that the LORD has cut with you on all these terms."

They Ate and They Drank

9And Moses went up, and Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel.

10And they saw the God of Israel, and under His feet was something like brickwork of sapphire, like the very body of the sky for purity.

11And the nobles of the sons of Israel He did not strike down. And they looked upon God, and they ate and they drank.

Forty Days in the Cloud

12And the LORD said to Moses, "Come up to Me on the mountain, and be there, and I will give you the tablets of stone — the instruction and the commandment — which I have written to teach them."

13And Moses rose, and Joshua his attendant, and Moses went up to the mountain of God.

14And to the elders he said, "Stay here for us until we return to you. And here — Aaron and Hur are with you. Anyone with a dispute, take it to them."

15And Moses went up the mountain, and the cloud covered the mountain.

16And the weight of the LORD's glory settled on Mount Sinai, and the cloud covered it six days. And on the seventh day He called to Moses from inside the cloud.

17And the look of the LORD's glory was like a consuming fire on the top of the mountain, before the eyes of the sons of Israel.

18And Moses went into the middle of the cloud and went up the mountain. And Moses was on the mountain forty days and forty nights.

Notes

  • vv3, 7 "we will do" … "we will do, and we will listen" — the people answer twice, and the second answer is longer by one word. In v3 it is na'aseh, we will do. In v7, after the book has been read out, it is na'aseh ve-nishma, we will do and we will hear — agreement first, understanding second, in that order. That fuller form is the famous one. It is also what the Greek already has back at 19:8, where the Hebrew has only we will do: one of the two traditions puts the full pledge at the start of the Sinai account, the other holds it back until the terms have actually been read.

  • v4 "twelve standing stones" — matzevot, and one chapter ago, at 23:24, the same word carried a command: you shall utterly break their standing stones. The pillar is the standard object of Canaanite worship, and Moses sets up twelve of them at the foot of the mountain on the morning the covenant is ratified. The text neither defends this nor notices it.

  • v5 "he sent the young men" — na'arei, not priests. Aaron is standing right there and is not the one who offers. The priesthood does not exist yet; it is legislated four chapters later. The sacrifices that seal the covenant are made by unnamed young men.

  • vv6, 8 the blood is divided — half into basins, half thrown against the altar, and then the basins' half thrown on the people. The altar stands for one party and the crowd is the other, and the same blood goes onto both. Nothing else in the Torah does this; blood is normally put on an altar, an object, or a priest, never flung over a congregation.

  • v8 "the blood of the covenant" — dam ha-berit, which the Greek renders to haima tēs diathēkēs. At the last supper, over the cup, Matthew has Jesus say τοῦτο γάρ ἐστιν τὸ αἷμά μου τῆς διαθήκης — this is my blood of the covenant (26:28). The phrase is this verse's, word for word in Greek, with one word added.

  • v10 "brickwork of sapphire" — livnat ha-sappir, and livnah is the ordinary word for a brick: the thing Israel was making in Egypt with mortar and straw in 1:14 and 5:7. The pavement under God's feet is described with the word for the item these men spent their lives producing as slaves, now made of precious stone. (The stone itself is sappir, which in this period most likely names lapis lazuli rather than what a jeweler today calls sapphire; the identification cannot be settled from the language.)

  • v10 "like the very body of the sky" — ke-etzem ha-shamayim, and etzem is bone. Hebrew uses it for the substance of a thing, the thing itself — the same idiom behind on that very day. What is under His feet is the sky's own bone, for clearness. The verse describes the floor and says nothing whatever about what they saw above it.

  • v11 "He did not strike them down" — lo shalach yado, literally He did not send His hand, and the Hebrew is an idiom rather than a gesture: to send the hand against someone is to strike them. It is the phrase God uses at Genesis 22:12, do not lay a hand on the boy. So the verse is not reporting that God kept still; it is reporting that He did not strike them — which takes for granted that seeing Him should have been fatal, and says so only by denying it. Then seventy-four men have a meal on the mountain. In 33:20 God will tell Moses that no one can see His face and live; this chapter says these men saw Him and ate.

  • v11 "the nobles" — atzilei, and the word is genuinely unsettled. It occurs three times in the Hebrew Bible and means something different in each: the joints of the arm at Ezekiel 13:18, the far corners of the earth at Isaiah 41:9, and here, a group of men. What ties them is the root atzal, to set aside, reserve — the verb God uses in Numbers 11:17 when He takes some of the spirit that is on Moses and reserves it for these same seventy elders. The men are named in v9; the noun for them means the ones set apart.

  • v14 "anyone with a dispute" — ba'al devarim, literally a master of words, and in Hebrew that is not a talker: it is the party to a lawsuit, the man who has a matter to argue. Moses leaves the court running while he is gone, with Aaron holding it. The next time Aaron is asked to handle the people on his own, in chapter 32, it goes differently.

  • v16 "six days… and on the seventh day He called" — the cloud covers the mountain for six days and the voice comes on the seventh. The pattern is the creation week's, and nothing in the verse points at it; the shape is simply there, at the moment the plan for the sanctuary is about to be given.
